div.head: TON'S
div.p: TON'S
COFFEE ESSENCE
PAVLOVA.

Mine. Anna Pavlov, the greatest of all Russian ballerini, is distinguished in real life by the unaffected charm of her manner end the quietness of her dress. She is a cultnred woman, speaks French perfectly, talks fluent English with a delicious Russian accent, and prefers to live as simply as possihle. The moment she goes on to the stage, she is transfigured. She becomes intoxicated with the music of Chopin or Glazunoff and, apparently without effort, is a vision of exquisite grief or of mad enjoyment. The pathos of her dancing of the " Passing of the Swan ' is extraordinary. The madness and impetuous energy with which she rushes through the famous Bacchanalian dance is impassioned to the verge of frenzy. The truth is that she is as great an actress as she is a dancer. The critics who wrote of her recent performance at Covent Garden, • where she had, as usual, a wonderful triumph, have been unanimous in recognising this. They were echoing, without knowing it, the opinions of the critics of St Petersburg and Paris. Perhaps the greatest testimony to the supreme genius of Pavlova is to be found in the ease with which she has conquered audiences differ- ing entirely in character. She roused enthusiasm in the United States as he did in Sweden and in Finland. Berlin, Prague, Vienna, Copenhagen gave her an equally enthusiastic welcome. The aristocratic audience at Covent Garden was moved to the same pitch of excite- ment as the more democratic audience of the Palace Theatre. The truth is that Pavlova unites to wonderful technique the quality of genius. One forgets the diffi- culties of the steps she executes in sheer delight at the effect of effortless motion and lightness she produces. She poises herself so lightly in Le Pepillo "of Drigo that the audacity of a human being trying to represent the fluttering grace of a tutterfiy is forgotten. She gives a new beauty to the music of Chopin. In our generation there has been no dancer like her and it is a great gain that she has decided to reveal the beauty of her art to those who cannot come to London to see her. Pavlova is booked to appear at, the Shakespeare Theatre. Liverpool, for the week commencing Monday September f:3rd.

The publications of Messrs Gertons, Limited, the well-known scientific farm plant breeders, of ‘Varring- too, are always interesting reading, and their latest issue of a booklet entitled "New and regenerated breeds of wheats" is no exception to this rule. In this publication some notable successes are given, gained by Messrs Gartons new and regenerated breeds in trials made in connection with various agricultural colleges throughout the ceuntry. These trials in some instances show an increased value of no less than .£2 us lid per acre in favour of the new end regenerated breeds over the average of other varieties. Although the weather recently experienced has been by no means favourable for the production of good samples of wheats, Messrs Gartons are nevertheless, owing to their growing their seeds in the best seed producing counties of England, Scotland and Ireland able to offer samples of excellent quality and of full germination. In a season like the present one the distribution of their contracts for seed purposes gives then, a great advantage of which their customers will derive full benefit. Winter oats, winter barleys and varin us other seeds for autumn sowing are also quotes and fully described in this publication.

div.head: Warrington's New Half Back,
div.p: Warrington's New Half Back,

One inducement which took me to Leigh was the first appearance in Lancashire of Rushton,Warrington's new half-back. Ile was said to have given a fair dis- play at Huddersfield, and some thiug better was expected on Saturday. Well ! I don't want to be guilty of a hasty and perhaps unfair judgment of the man Warrington have paid a pretty stiff price for but unless he was ill or had some equally good excuse for the form displsyed on Saturday. he is mot first team class ! Added to Rushton's feebleness was the fact that Brooks tried to play the Leigh thirteen single- handed and got tackled with the ball times innumer- able. I should think he gave his centres about two passes each all afternoon. It was a `orricl spectacle for supporters of the Wirepullers !

The forwards were overweighted but they were never badly beaten for possession, and they excelled in the loose. They can easily be stiffened where necessary. The great weakness is at half, and on the wings. Clare is another man who is out of his element in first-class football, and the sooner it is realised and the better. He he not improved an atom in the last twelve months. Renwick and Dickensn have both played better, but they saved the team from a seveter licking.

The rne bright spot was the display of young Jolley at full back. He played a brilliant game, and earned the warmest praise all round the ground. The lad is such a fine natural footballer that I still feel the best of him is not seen at full back. With his dodging ability and resource he should make an ideal halfback, and nothing would please me better than to see him operating behiiid the pack with Mclntyre in the rear position.

Leigh are still a strong lot forward, but they are poor on the attack. Roberts and Donohue make a promising wing, and Sam Johnson is both sound and clever at full back, but the team as st present con- stituted will not go far. Like Warrington they are badly served at half back.

I am told that Warrington's juniors shaped like juniors at home on Sttnrday and were both over- weighted and out-pointed by the Leigh lads. Neither Moore nor Dixon distinguished themselves, the latter being very slow and disappointing. The best display was given by Twist. the Widnes wing, alio ran very speaddy and strongly,and tackled with certainty every time. He seems to have the makings of a good three- quarter. Warrington have apparently got a long row to hoe in building up a local team, but they deserve every encouragement.

Everybody is hoping to see Warrington byeak the proverbial 'duck" to-clay, when they oppose Broughton Rangers at Wilderspool. The first. league match of the season should draw a big crowd and if it does not end in a handsome win for the Wire- pullers there will be vast disappointment. Last Saturday the Rangers were only able to halve the points at home with Leeds.

The Warrington side has one or two changes in it which make for strength. Thomas returns to the for- wards in place of Crirchley, and as he has been train- ing hard be sh,uld soon make his presence felt. When in form the Welshman has few superiors, and be cannot well be spared from the Warrington pack as long as he is fit. Clare stands down from the wing and Twist the Widnes lad receives early opportunity of showirg his metal. Mclntyre has also reported for duty and rakes the place of Dickenson, who hurt his knee last Saturday. Rushon is 0 have another trial. 'rhe selected team is : , Jolley, full back ; Waywell, Mclntyre, Renwick and Twist, three-quarters ; Brooks and Rushton, half- backs; Thomas, Cheaters, Tranter, Skelborne, Fearaley and Arnold, forwards.

For the Rangers against Warrington. Barlow will play at half-back instead of Tighe, and R Clampitt joins the list of possible forwards. Team : llanson, full back ; Scott, Barnes, Harris (Capt.) and Davirlson, three-quarters ; Barlow and Jones, half backs; Clarrpitt Gorry, Winskill, Hirst, Clampitt (R.), Cheetham and Roberts, forwards.
Shugars is back in town again, and lnoks fit and well but an injury in training at home will keep him . . out of the game for a week or two.

Warrington "A " team has also urdergone con- siderable alteration, Moore has got a cold, and stands down, while Brown returns to the full back positions. Two new local three-quarters in Wel6lay and Davies, both converts from the Association code, are on trial, and Berry, the young Wigan half back, is also turning out. Some very favourable opinions have been formed of the local " soccer " men, and I hope they will fulfil-anticipations. The team will be well-tried at Wheaters Field. The full side is: _
11,own, full back; Povey, Dixon, Welsby and Davies, three-quarters; Jordan and Berry, half backs ; Valentine, Bevan, 13randwood, Cooper, Gibbs and Critchley, forvral ds.

Warrington's Poor Display at Leigh.

The Warriogton men opened the season with a visit to Leigh and sustained defeat. by *narrow margin after a poor game. The weather was beautifully flue until the last 20 minutes and a crowd of quite 4 WC/assembled round the Mather-lane ground. Ruth teams were as selected arid turned out as follows : Warrirgton.—Jolley, hack ; Clare, Renwick, LYcken- son and Waversll, threequarter-backs ; Brooks and Rushton, half-backs ; Skelhorn, Trauter, Fear'sley, Critchley, Arnold and Cheaters, forwards Leigh.—S Johnson, back ; Neville, T H Johnson, Roberts and Donohue, threequarter.backs ; Cain tenti Mooney, half-hacks ; Lee, Lowe, Davies, Melting, Barton and Cartwright, forwards. Referee, Mr A Hestford, Broughton ; touch-judges, Messrs E Williams, Widnes, and W V‘allwork, Swinton. Warriugton were fortunate to win the toss and have the advautage of a strong breeze in the first half. Leign opened strongly in the scrimmages and made a brief raid to the Warrington end where Jolley cleared nicely. Tranter and Skelhorn led the way to the other end with a dashing run, and Leigh were hard pressed. Neville made a weak attempt to clear with a cross-kick which resulted in the home backs getting offside. Renwick took the penalty kick and lauded an easy goal for Werrington. 'lbis early score to Warrington was heartily cheered by their supporters, rind tor a time they looked like getting a useful lead. Brooks and Dicksnsou got ready on the left, arid a capital opening was made for Clare. The wing men took the pass but seemed slow in starting and was quickly overhauled by Donohue. Leigh pleyed up strongly after this and I y good forwero work they forced Warrington t.r denim . Renwick cleared finely on one occasion and Jolley followed up a punt which almost caused disaster. 'the ball was forced past the Warrington toll back before he could get into position and row Johnson dribbled half the length of the 11.-Id tee balk just roll- , ing in touch near the Warringloa line. Leigh raerdel desperate elferts to get Over acid in the melee jolly , was "knocked out";:nd equired attention on the touch- line. A fine emit ty Reowick citared the way to the Leigh half where Sam Johoson'S kick was charged down and Trenter tail on the ball inches short of the line Mooney relieved pressure rind the interval came with Wistriegtori leading by 2 paints to nil. Leib resumed with any annatet of confidence and Donohue early had a shot at goal which failed. War- rington reevaided with Stuart forward play ond there seemed a prospect of better things when Brooks took a pass from Rushton at half way and got meta with Waywell in attendance. Brooks ten strongly but spoiled the effort by throwing to VCaywell when the latter was completely covered by Neville. A short hick might have had a different result. Leigh soon changed the venue and Sam John- son equalised with a dropped goal from. a clearing punt by Brooks. Play was now hotly contested, though chiefly of a scrambling character, and Arnold MS absent injured for a quarter of an hour. This weakened Warrington's already light forwards, and a prolonged attack resulted in Cain receiving from a scrum on the line acid running over with the only try of the day. Donohue bit the cross-bar with his goal kick. Warring- ton had the worst of matters to the end, and Donohue would have scored in the last five minutes, but for a great tackle by Jolley. Final : Leigh, 1 goal 1 try k 5 points) ; Warrington, 1 goal (2 points). RUNCORN WIN AT COVENTRY.

About 2,500 spectators saw Coventry open their third season, at home, with a match against Runcorn. The Midland men were inferior in size to their opponents, and were pressed most of the time, while they had the additional disadvantage of losing their full back after 20 minutes play. Lewis started the scoring for the visitors, and lonian and Hughes followed, while just before half-tirde Coventry had a penalty try given against them for obstruction. Winter getting over for tie home team, the score at the interval was 11 points to 3. Although Parkinson was unable to return to the field, Coventry made a plucky stand throughout, and in the second half (when a try on either side was added) the game was MOTO even. Coventry occasionally did well at forward, arid put in a few brilliant bouts at passing. Runcorn did best in the scrummages, and showed good combination. Result :—Runcorn 1 goal 4 tries (14 points), Coventry 2 tries 16 points). Teams and officials : Coventry.—Parkinson, back ; Winter, Dakin, Carter. and Littlewood, three-quarter becks; Beynou and Davies, half backs; Oldham,Tomes, Hutt, Browo,Wood, and Johnson forwards. Runcorn—Shaw back: Whitfield, Moran, Moores, and Hughes, iheee-quarter hacks ; Lewis and Steele, half backs ; Richardson, Kirkham, Inman, Stevenson, Massey, and Padhury, forwards. Referee Mr W It Hirst, Dewsbury. Touch judges, Messrs Johnson, Salford, and Jones, Warrington. WIDNES v. SWINTON : LAW'S FINE DISPLAY. Played at, Widnes before 3,000 spectators. Widnes gave a very promising display, Laws especially playing a great game. On one occasion he ran rigut through the thick of his opponents from half way and scored. Taylor opened the scoring for Widnee by placing a goal. The same player made a nice opening, and subse- quent passing by Laws and Lally ended in the latter scoring. Laws initiated a passing movement which ended in Cosgrove scoring, and then a mull by Johnson let in Lloyd. Taylor intercepted a pass and gave to Reid, who raced over at the corner. Just before the Interval Price scored an unimproved try for Swinton. The only score in the second half was a try by Laws, Result :—Vvidnes 1 goal 5 tries (17 paints), Swinton 1 try (3 points). Teams and officials :- 1 Widnn—Jones, back ; Laws, Lally, Taylor, and Swinton. three-quarter backs ' • Moon and O'Clarra, half I backs ; G Aspey' S Aspey, Lloyd, Cosgrove, Higgins, and Reid, forwards. Swinton—J ohnson.,back ; Brookes.Frodsham,Dawson, and Gartrell, three-quarter backs ; Jones and Moores, bait backs •, Dan Davies, Randall, McVeigh, Preston, Price, and Pollitt, forwards. Reteree, Mr J F May, St Helens. Touch judges, Mersrs If Turner, Warrington, and T Austin, Wigan. Sr. HELENS v. BARROW. Barrow journeyed to St. Helens and played without Morgan for a large psrt of the game, he being injured. There were 6,000 spectators. In the first half Barrow were superior forward. Greenwood scored a try for the home team, which Turtill converted, Turtill also getting a penalty goal, while Barrow could only respond with a penalty goal from Mitchell. In the second half the home forwards improved, and Mavitty and Browning scored unconverted tries, Molyneux kioking a penalty goal. St. Helens took more advan- tage of their chances than Barrow did of theirs, but in adopting the open game the home team were unsuc- cessful. Result :—St Helens 3 goals 3 tries (15 points), Barrow 1 goal 2 tries (8 points). div.head: WARRINGTON WORKS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKS ASSOCIATION.
FLETCHERS' MOULDERS Will FINLAYSON

After many weeks, the great competition organised by the Watrington Works Association reached the climax on Saturday, when the final match, which had been p3stponed from August 24tJ, between Fletcher's Moulders aid Howley Tannery was decided. Through- out the whole competition one spirit of fie( y enthusiasm has prevailed and the public generally have greatly interested themselves in the doings of tne various teams. 'the teams have contested for the handsome trophy given by Mr. John Finlays-n atd the gold medals provide.] by the Association, in a thorough sportsmanlike and gentlemanly manner, and the competition on the whole hss been a d-q.tided succe4s, chiefly owing to the energies of the oflioials with Mr, Patrick as secretary, who have worked most assiduously together from the b-ginni. g. There was a large attendance of spectators on the Horse and Jockey Green on Saturday to witness the final which promised so much in the way of excitement. _ THE SCENE OF ENGLAND'S LAST BATTLE. Or rather, the last battle fought on English soil, for among other countlies in the south, S, meiset carries us thiough some famous scenes in English history, and we passed through a goad many of them the Saturday before August Monday. It was a beautiful morning when V., e bet off eastwards from Dunster, almost the last morning of the kind for a month. At Washfurd I ran up a iide lane to see on what terms we c ,uld get through Cleeve Abbey. When I found that another shilling would be needed, I remembered Coverhaiu Abbey in Yorkshire, for this looked like a farm house too. When you pay a shilling to see an abbey and bare to pick out the carved stones, beautiful as they may be, out of the coal house wall, or take a riddle down off a peg to see a gargoyle, it takes away a good deal of the poetry of the thing. So we played nap for once, and passed. The long rise over the edge of the Quantocks is rewarded with a spec aid series of views over the Bristol Channel, with the di staut islands and the mountains of Glamorgan. The road doesn't seem able to make up its mind whether to dart for the top of the hills or not, hut at Nether S tou-ey it filially leaves them fr its long flat journey- over Sedgrnere I picked up a dead viper from the bract en by the edge of the rood, evidently just able to crawl there after being completely crushed across by some cart or niche probably a motor. As we drew near Bridgry ttor a string of motor cycles raised clouds of (last, and rs tb-ey were scttiug out f :ir a race, no: too considerate for mere p“.l4llers. Another lis orical touch is given by Bridgwater which has rt cently added to its mans' attractions a fine statue of Admiral Blake, for it was his birthplace. Instead of taking the main r tad to Glastonbury al, rig the Folden ridge we crossed the battk field to Weston Zl.rd It w-g close by he.. In the Isle of Ailielney where the famous jaw el of King Alfred was found, now k-p; at the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford. W hat a distria this is for a lover 'of history ! A contrast indeed now with its rich corn- fields, from when Alfred watched the cakes birning, a contrast even greater from that day's fight described in Lorna Boone when the poor fool 'Monmouth lust his cause against James IL in IGBS. And what a happy country ours is. now tray, Pig its third century with- out the s mud of fighting armies. Every place name in this p trt of Somerset bears toe Anglo--raxort starnp.and a cety full week could be sp-nt by a hi lilay maker between the Quantock Hilts and Mendips. All the
The Examiner, Saturday, September 14, 1912.
Church of their birth and their love—they could not return to the bosom of the Estahlisbment. But even if the Act were repealed, they would 134ve to
ALTER THE: WHOLE cON-CEPTIoN OF THE CHRISTIAN CHURCH, . _ . .

before they could conscientionsly conform. Their Puritan fathers stood for the spiritual conception of the Christian Church. He (the speaker) did not care what creed a man held ; creeds only intellectually diflerenti sted then. No Nonconformist,if he were true to his convictions, could be a bigot. it be were a bigot, it wss because he had a sheer love of bigotry and in spite of the principles he held. The fundamental conviction of all the Free Churches was that vt herever Christian men and women met for worship and Christian service, I there Christ is, and the presence of Christ constituted I them a Christian Cauroh. If thtt were their funda- mental belief, they could not cherish narrow and exclusive prejudices ; they were bound to recognize as Caristian men and as Christian Churches those who might widely c llt r from them both in their intellectual beliefs and in their ecclesiastical polity and in their forms and modes of Christian worship and w rrk. They believed that the Church of Christ was a spiritual institution and that it ought to have no alliance with the State. Our Lord's words were proof of it : "My Kingdom is not of this world." He sharply differentiated, as to their origir, nature, prin- ciples and stability, between the Kingdoms of this world and His own spiritual Kingdom. " Render unto Cerar the things that are C•4sar's, and unto God the things that are God's." He (the speaker) could not conceive for a moment that Jesus Christ would regard as among the things of Cresar appointments to Bishoprics and chief pastorates over His own Church. For three centuries the Church was free from all the trammels of the State, and those who knew Church history would reclgnise that that was the era of the Church's greatest triumph. It vanquished ancient philosophy and ancient vice ; it. studded the civilized world with Christian churches, and its march of prc- gress was never arrested. But when Constantine annexed the Churc4, covering it with his imperial purple,so that he might be master of the Church as well a= lord of the State, did the Church gain anything ? No, it kat infinitely by that alliance with the State. Its lustre began to dim' and the SS of tile Middle Ages nettled like the pall of night :7er Ev.repe and was only dispersed by the dawn of the Reformation. They had been taught. by Christ, and they had teen confirmed in their belief by the teaching of history, that Christianity made its way best when it was left alone by the State. It needed no temporal arms to support it; the weapons of their war- fare were not carnal but spiritual. It was idle to suppose, as some Churchmen did, that

• -IE1:111C STATE CHURCH' WERE DISESTABZ.ISII/M in England as well as in Wales—and unless the trend of all civilisation in Europe misled there, the time could not be far distant when England as well as Wales would have a Free Church in a Free State—it was fzolish to fear that England would relapse into paganism, if the bond which united the (Thurch with the State and crippled the freedom of the Church were snapped asunder. lie (the speaker) knew that Bishop Welldon, Dean of Manchester, held th it view, because he had a controversy with him on the subject in the columns of the " Times." ! Voluntaryism had filled Wales with Noncon- formist chapels. It was a nation of Noncot- formists who clamoured for equality and brotherhood. Take cur self-governing COonies, There WLI3 JaCt tat Church Church in one of t: en arid y,t hrivturd t 3 ay that Christianity had as great a hold on our great Colonies as it had on the motherland. What made Eog'and a Christian nation? Not as Bishop Welldon supposed, the elistence of a State Church in our midst. A nal.ion was only Chrittian when the people who com- posed it were Christian. Let the spirit of Christ per- vade the hearts and lives of the people and then England would be in reality, r.s it was in name, a Christian land—and not one moment sooner. But sup2osing that the Act of Uniforraity were repealed and t...e State Church disestablished, even then they would hive to alter their whole conception of the Christian m:nistry before they could conscientEusly conform, because they

DID NOT DELIEVE IN A yinIAN If they took the Old Testament, written under the Jewish economy, they found there priests, sacrifices and altars, hut when they came to the New Testament they had neither the word nor the thing that the word •` priest" symbo- 14ed. Whether a man were an Anglican or a Noncon- formist, if he were honest in his scholarship he was bound to admit that the word " priest " in the New Testament was only used in one of two senses—either on the one hand, as applicable to Jesus Christ alone, tne sole Mediator of the Christian Caurch, or as applic• ale to the universal brotherhood of believers. The man who wrote the New Testament, Jesus Himself and bra apostles, were all trained under a sacerdotal system. They were familiar with the routine of the temple, with altars and sacrifices, but when they came ti establish the Christian religion they eliminated the whole vocabulary of sacerdotalism. If Christ had ' meant His ministers to be a sacerdotal erste, the apostles would base- been the first selected and it was of the very essence of priesthood to magnify its office. But those earliest bishops or posters—tor the words were synonymous in the New Testament—reared DO altars, ware no copes or mitres, offered no sacrifices, except those beautiful saorilices of praise and prayer. Not only was the silence of the New Teattruent significant upon that point, hut the whole spirit and teaching of the New Testament was absolutely destruc- tive ot the priestly conception of tbe ministry. They saw the present trend in the Establislud Church. Was it in the direction of the evangelical conception of the ministry—that was to soy, the conception in the New Testament which made the minister the spiritual leader and friend of the congregation ? Or was it in the direction of sacerdotalisru, which endowed a lawman being with supernatural gifts, enanling him to transmute a few drops of water into the channels c f regeueratinc grace, to turn the bread of the Lord's table, into the Body of Christ, and giving hint ability to pronounce absolution and remission of sin? The woole trend of the Church of England to-day—and he said it with profound sorrow—was away from the evangelical and towards the sacredotal conception of the ministry. But even if the drift of the Church were towards the evangelical conception of the ministry, Nonconformists would still have to alter their whole conception of Christian truth before they could conscientiously conform. They

DID NOT BELIEVE IN RCM AN CREEDS. They never asked those who were admitted into their membership to sigh a creed; they did not ask their ministers to assent to one. They believed that the mind of men ought 0 be tree, that the only authority which ought to bind a Christian was the authority of Christ. Ile quite admitted that the creeds of Christendom were historic monuments and were intereging trom tbat point of vi!,w, but they had no binding authority upon human minas and consciences. He thought tie had said enough to show that Non3onformity was rooted in the earn° religious convictions to-day as were held by their Puritan fathers w!,en they sacrificed everything dear to !hem in this lire in order to have a conscience unsullied in the sight of God. Puritanism stood for that which was noblest in the nation's life and ideals and he wanted the young people of the Free Churches to show the same fidelity to conscience and the same following of truth nod freedom as did thise great [urn whose heroic Bacrifice they had been commemorating.

div.head: GREAT EJECTIYIENT.
div.p: THE GREAT EJECTIYIENT.
UNITED MEETING OF FREE CHURCHMEN AT CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL.
NONCONFORMISTS AND THE CHURCH.

Cairo-street Chapel, which was established by Robert Yates, the ej-cted minister of the Warrington Parish Church, and is consequently the home of Nonconformity in Warrington, was, last Sunday even- ing, the berme of a remarkable gathering. The occasion was a united service of Nooconformist con- gregations, held to commemorate the Ejectment of 1662, and it was made r-inarkable by the fact that it was held in a chapel which, though really free, is c3rnuaonly regarded as Unitarian, and consequently not always welcomed to assoLqation with other Nonconformist bodies. The hervice was a truly undenorniuntional one, practically all the Non- conformist bodies being represented, and the following miLiEters took ptit in toe service : Rev Jr Mellor, minister of Cairo-street Chapel, Rev W Reid, St John's Presbyterian, Rev H Oder, Baptist, Mr A Mounfi-ld, Independent Methodist, Rev J J Glover, Risley Presbyterian, who presided, and Rev G E Cheeseman, Congregationalist, I who Llivet ed the addre..,s. Through:ut the service, emphasis W3B laid on the urrectarian aspect of the occasion, and the congregation which filled the old chapel t 3 overflowi .g, could hardly fail to be imprebsea by the feeling of belonging, at least for a time, to that wider community ot the Church which recognises no denominational barriers. It is the sincere hope of those who organized the service that I,ooy lead to a still greater unity amongst the various " Fre) emr:h-s ia ktiar:ingtoi, and perhaps prove to be almost historic as st:p L:wards bridging over denominational differences. . .

LIBERAL CLUB BOWLING OEFICIALS. Mr. F. Walker (secretary) and Mr. Jospli Wilkinson (president).

Many ardent bowling enthusiasts are to be found amongst local Liberals and the play on the beautiful BewSey-sfteet Oreen is always of a good character. Mains are arranged and played off quite smoothly and the secretary of the bowling green, Mr. Walker, is deserving of every praise for the exce.lent services he has rendered and the untiring ‘‘ay in which he has worked to make this particular branch of the Assoc,ation's wcrk a huge success, as indeed it is. The President of the bowling green,, M-. Joseph Wilkinson, has also rendered in valuable assistance and has taken a keen interest in the doings of the trundiers throughout the competiti .us. In the annual dosing main which was finished on Saturday. there were TO entries and the various games have been of a very interesting nature. The playera have the privilege of playing on one of the finest green in th-i town, the splendid condition being one to the energ;es expended by Mr. Clay, tl whom the players are indeed grateful. The games on Saturday vere witnessed by a large number of spectators and the prize winners were : 1, S Riley ; 2, W Taylor; 3, \V Warburton ; 4, E A Sanders ; 5, J Gibson ; 6, T O'Brien, 7, J Parr; S. watercourses or drains as they are called run in straight lines along the roadsides, and are ornamented with pollard willows at either side. Growing in the water we found quantities of two beautiful wild plants, the arrow head, and the 11 .wering rush, the latter a particularly fine adornment of those long straight drains. At Glastonbury- they were repairing an ancient bridge over the River Brue, and had just unearthed several courses of Roman stonework. I suppose Glastonbury Abbey would rot have been so disappointing if the fame and expectation of great things had been less. Like Kirkstall Abbey near Leeds it is being propped up wiih yards of new stone work, but the architect is putting the date of these restorations on each patch of his NV ,rk so that Ifacaulay's New Zealander shall not be deceived when he has paid his half dollar. It is eel tainly an abbey well worth visiting by those who love legends and history. The original church was budt by Joseph of Arimithea, sr the le;end runs. Whether he lust his staff or not I clo9't know, but it grew into a hawthorn tree in the Alit ey grounds, and , its haegs are represented now by the Holy Thorn near the gateway. Whatever truth may lie in that story, the record exists of Edward I. visiting this abbey in 1278 to see the bones (reputed) of Eing Arthur and his Queen Guinevere placed in a shrine before the high altar. We finished the day's ride at Wells, in a downpour of rain that lasted 10.. g into tie next morning. *

div.p: THE ONTARIO CROP REPORT,

based upon returns of Government correspondents in various parts of the province, shows that farmers will get good returns for their labour. Particularly does this apply to fruit farmers. Grapes give promise ot a large )ield, and the increase of attention given by farmer i epraying and other modern features of orcharding has produced good results. lhere will be a fair yield of barley in nearly every county in the province. Oats have developed into a Bret-class crop, peas and .beans are up to the average, and there is a fair crop of hay of good quality all over the province ; potatoes promise good yields and roots are fair; livestock are in a good hesit.by condi- tion ; cattle are in brisk &mend at good prices. It is stated that. harvesting has been delayed owing to the ' lack of farm la-our, whici is rmulted to be as scare or scarcer than ever. Farmers are treing to meet the shortage of help by using larger iniplements and im- proved machinery, Interchanging labour with neigh- bours and doing more grazing. There are excellent prospects for experienced farm labouters, who are so scarce that very exceptional wages are being paid. Good men have been offered £8 per month, with board, for an engagement from April to November, while for a yearly engagement RA per month upward, with board, can be secured.

influence and power of Nonconformity. All branches of the Christian Church owed something to those 2,000 men who left the Cuurch because they felt they could only wo,ship God according to the dictates of their own consciences, lie feared that in thase they were sometimes apt to forget the self-sacrifice of those men into whose labours th,y had entered. He hoped that as the result of that meeting they would be kindled anew to fresh enthusiasm and to faithfulness in the crest work to which thy had been called. Toe Ref. G. it. CITEESF.AI AN gave a highly interesting end inspiring address. At the outset he said his task had been rendered easier by some remarkable articles in the lATirtiogton Examiner," waich were both illuminating end suggestive. Perhaps it was an open secret what authorship was concealed under the initials " A.NI." but he (the speaker) could say he had read those able, historic summaries of the Ejectment, in so far as it affected their own locality, with interest and profit and he would like to thank the author, in his own name and on behalf of that meeting, for his able contrieu- tious. Coetinuing the speaker said he hoped no wird would he said by him to wound the susceptibilities cf Church people. He had no hostility to the Established Cnurch—inderd some of the dearest friendships of his life were amoegse its clergy, and his brother was Rector of one of its parishes. He confessed he was not insensible to the claim which the Church of England had upon every EDglishuten's resp,ct. It had rooted itself in our national life. The course of English history would certainly have been different, but for the action of Nonconformity 001 our national character and life, but the same was equally true of the Anglican Church. The history of England would have been different, if it had not been tor the impact of that great Church upon cur national life. The liturgy of the Church of England was incomparable-' it was the heirloom of the Caristial ages. He himself used it in his public devotions in the church ; he recognised no monopoly in those inimitable prayers, as vehicles of devotion. The researches of their scholars were common property. Scholarship knew no denominational limitations and just as Nonconformity was enriched by the scholars of the Church, so the Church of England was enriched by great scholars and theologians of Nonconformity like Dr. Fairbairn and Dr. Dale. But while he (the speaker) loved the Church of England and would not see, a word to injure or out- rage the sneceptibilities of any Churchman, he must say he preferred Nonconformity. He was still a staunch and loyal Nonconformist and, if he were asked to justify his Nonconformity, he said that the very reasons which made their fathers Nonconformists and

impelled them to Facrilice thitr livings at the call of conscience, made and kept their succssqors Non- conformists to-day. The Act of Uniformity was unrepealed. That Act was the end of a long series of Acts, the intention of uhich was, in the words of one of the historians of the day, to "harry the Puritans out of the land " Why did they object to the Puritans? Demme the Puritans WANTED TO REFORM THE CHURCH FROM WITHIN.

They wanted to make it more after the New 'lestament model. The speaker gave several illustrations to prove that in all . the protests of the Puritans there were real principles at stake. The Savoy Con ferecce met to consider the Puritan objections, but: Bishop Burnett told us. in the history of his own times, that it was the intention of the Bishops to make the terms of conformity stricter than hPf ore, and li:shop Sheldon, in his coarse fashion, said: "Now we know the minds of the Puritans we will make them knaves if they conform." That was the spirit of the dominant faction in the Church of England and the result ens that the Act of Uniformity was passed. It was passed in the teeth of royal promises and against the %ishes of both Houses of Convocation. That Act stated that every vicar or holder of any benefice in the Church of England must, on some Lord's Day before St. Bartholomew's Day, 1662, declare his unfeigned assent and consent t ;everything contained in the Book of Common Prayer. St. Bartholomew's Day was chosen because on that day the tithes of the past year fell due and so, if the Puritans would not conform, they must not only be ejected from their livings, but they must lose the tithes that were then legally due to them. But to the honour of their Puritan fathers be it said, more than 2,000 of them gave up their livings at the call of conscience and went, home- less wanderers, into the world. So long as the Act of Uniformity remained unrepealed on the statute book— that Act which drove their fathers out and followed them with penal laws when they were exiled from the

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

THE INSURANCE ACT. TUBERCULOSIS DISFENSARY AT ST. HELENS. JOENT SANATORIUM SUGGESTED. At the St Helens Health Committee on Wednesday the Deputy Town-clerk (Mr. Turton) read a letter from the Local Government Board approving, under section 16 of the National Insurance Act, for a period of six mouths from July 15th last, of the tuberculosis dis- pensary at the Town Hall, the Borough Ssnaturium, and the old Whint Hospital. The Board expressed the opinion that before a permanent scheme was adopted ior the treatment of tuberculosis in the county borough, further consideration should be given to the questions of rie etaciency of the qualiflcetions of the tuberculosis officer appointed by the 'rown C,uncil, and of the salary assigned to the office. Tne Board was glad t le .ru that the Town Council proposed to no-operate with other authorities for the provision of a sinatorium and they thought that the question whether the permanent dispensary proposed to be established in the county borough could not also serve some or the I adjoining areas should be discussed with the Lanoa- eht.r.o County Council.

Mr Forshaw said that as they in St. Helens bad taken steps to treat non-insured persons, they ought to take action early and apply for their quota of the cost. Dr Buchan (medical officer) said that the committee had spent about £l.OOO on tuberculosis already this year, and they would need to apply for half of that. The Chairman said the Parliamentary Committee had in band the negotiations with other. authorities for the erection of a tuberculosis sanatorium. They had two ' or three sites in view, and he wanted that committee to meet specially on that matter. The chief point they would have to consider was whether they would include in their scheme a sanatorium for curative purposes or if they would simply deal with chronic cases. Mr W Bates said that for some time they had been dealing with chronic cases, and they were wishful to combine with surrounding authorities on that matter. The Chairman said the joint sanatorium was intended to be for curative purposes. They bad a huge mass of information to deal with at the special meeting. The committee agreed to have a special meeting.

When Kate Leveson, an elderly Jewess, was charged on remand at Blackpool on Wednesday with alleged falsA preiences, she asked for legal aid, but when the Chief Constable said that she had recently purchased 4.:.100 worth of goods at Warrington, the Bench declined to grant her request. It was exphitined by the Chief Constable that defendant took a sitting-room and bedroom on Jaly 30th at the house of Mrs. Elizabeth Howarth. 12, Exchange-street, Blackpool, agreeing to pay 18s. a week. During her stay there she had obtained money from Mrs Howarth, and between August 6th and 30th she asked Mis Ilowaith if she wanted some stair carpet, which was worth s'a Gd a yard. Defendant said Robert Henry Lewtas had given her £2 t 4 getl some stair carpet, and that he bad got more than he wanted. On this representation Mrs Howarth gave defendant 10s to obtain some of the stair carpet, but it had since been I ound that defendant's statement about Lewtas was not true, and defendant was arrested. Elizabeth Howarth, a widow, residing at 12, Exchange-street, stated that defendant went to her house on July 30th and took rooms in the name of Mrs. Roberts, saying she was going to carry on the business of a dressmaker. Witness gave evidence in support of the Chief Constable's statement as to advancing 10s. for the stair carpet, and said she had not received the stair carpet nor the money back. In answer to the Chief Constable, witness said she had advanced sums of money to defendant at different times which amounted to about Robert Hy Lewtas, carriage proprietor, of Exchange street, gave evidence denying that he ever gave defendant any money to get stair carpet for. him, or that he had received any carpet from her. Detective Inspector Drabble, said that when he charged prisoner she said. "My God! What else are they going to levy against me? The Chief Constable said be had got two warrants; for the woman's arrest—from Warrington and Ramsgate for alleged fair prfences, the amountr involved at Warrington being i.ooo. The Mayor sent her to hard labour for three months

The Labour Party has A PRESENT TO made the Opposition THE OPPOSITION th 3 handsome present of the seat which was occupied by Mr Gladstone, Major Hope, the Conservative candidate, being returned by a majority of thirty-two votes over Mr Shaw. It is not much of a victory, from any point of view. Major-Hope has just scraped through, though Provost Brown, the Labour candidate carried off 2,413 votes, the whole of them de- ducted, as is quite plain on this occasion, from the normal Liberal poll. In 1910 the same Tory candidate polled 5,680 votes, and he now polls 6,021. Nobody expected that Ile would fait below his previous record, and he has exceeded it only by 341. Is this to be pro- claimed as a Conservative victory? In Midlothian, Conservatism stands much as it did in 1900. In that year Colonel Dalrymple- Hamilton polled 5,490 votes, but the Liberal poll with the Master of Elibank as candidate was then only 5,804. In 1906, the eldest son of LORD ROSEBERY was returned by 8,348. Here was an enormous advance in the num- ber of Liberal electors; but the deduction from the Tory poll was less than 700. In January, 1910, there was another advance in the Liberal poll to the high-water mark of 9,062, the Tory poll being 5,427. Major HOPE'S popularity with his party is proved by the fact that in December of the same year, 1910, he brought his party back to a higher position than it had held since it first lost the seat to the Liberals. He has improved on this, as we have said, by over 300. The difference is that he gets into Parliament; and that is a very great differ- ence, of course; but he gets in with 8,402 votes against his 6,021.

There are two things to be particularly noted. In the first place, Provost BROWN and Mr. ISHAI,v .between them have not received as much support as was given to the MASTER OF ELIBANK at the last election. When the totals are added together there is a falling off to the extent of 435 votes. It may be assumed that 300 of these have gone to Major HOPE. That would give him the whole of the increase in his total of 6,021. The remainder of the falling off, with some counterbalance to the natural increase in the number of electors, would be accounted for lby deaths and removals. It is certainly much clearer here than in most cases that there has been a shifting of votes from one party to the other. Its extent, as we have seen, is 341. This, then, may be said to be the• value of the attack on

the Insurance Act in a constituency like Edinburgh. Was the game worth the candle? The Conservative reply will, of course, be that it was. The seat has been won. Major HOPE takes the place of the MASTER OF EUBANK. His vote will count two in a division in thelHouse of Commons. But will he say in that House—will he be permitted to say, whatever his personal willingness might be—such things about the Insurance Act as he said in Midlothian? Will his party adoixt those proposals of amendment by which he seems to have gained 340 votes? If there can be one thing more certain than another, it is that the return of Major HOPE will have no effect whatever either on the present or the future of the Insurance Act.

Major HOPE enters the House with a majority of 2,381 against him—a poor result of a representative system. The majority in Midlothian finds the constituency repre- sented by a gentleman whom it has repudi- ated in what should have been an over- whelming manner. The Tory party has won singularly few seats since the last General Election, and its successes in that direction ' have all been owing to the assistance, in one way or another, of what is, with much inaccuracy, called the Labour vote, the bulk of working men having obviously, in this and other instances, voted some for the Liberal and some for the Tory candidate,since in every constituency, except the City of London and the constituencies which include the London squares, the working-class voters greatly preponderate in number. The one thing most clearly discernible in recent elections is that the Tory party is not making progress. The increase in its vote is abnormally small, considering that a Liberal Government has been in power since the end of 1905. The pendulum no longer swings. This means, surely, that the party is out of favour with the nation. And never- theless, it is every now and then getting a seat presented to it. This latest attack of the Labour Party was on an historic Liberal seat. Do the Labour men want a Conserva- tive Government back again, wit'.l its wars, its Licensing and its Education Bills, its extravagance in expenditure, its hostility to Labour itself, its jobs in every department of the State? If the answer to that question is in the negative, its conduct certainly stands in need of some explanation.

Electoral reform is GETTING VOTES! being tackled on bold an d comprehensive lines by the Government, and the days of Revision Courts are numbered. They will pass into oblivion " unwept, unhonoured and unsung" by the vast majority of electors, for the existing methods of regulating the franchise are cumbrous, irritating and full of anomalies. It is perhaps natural that revising Barristers should lament the dis- appearance of the regime under which they play such a prominent part, and Mr. C. H. M. Wharton, who has conducted the revision at Warrington this week, delivered himself of sundry criticisms of the Government measure. He cannot "realize the possibility of its passing" but we fail to see any ground for questioning the determination of the Government to sweep away a system which few would venture to defend. Even Mr. Wharton admits that ' there is much room for improvement and his chief grievance appears to be that revising barristers have not been consulted in the drafting of the Bill. The business of the Warrington Revision Court this year was comparatively light, and presented little of outstanding interest. The Conser- vatives raised a frivolous protest against the, notices of objection sent out by the Liberal agent, but it was promptly and emphatically over-ruled by the Barrister. There were several contentious cases, and the Liberal interests were carefully and efficiently watched by Mr. E. A. Sanders, who allowed no points to slip and was deservedly com- plimented by the Barrister upon the thoroughness with which he argued an important objection.

The Protectionists there are not going to have it all their own way. The Johannesburg Chamber of Commerce, for instance, has decided: .

"That -a- P-r-O-t-e-c-ti;e- Customs tariff is opposed to the interests of South Africa for the following reasons: (1) That one effect of the same now is, and must be for a long time to come, to increase the cost of living, and thus to discourage immigration and closer settlement; (2) That the tendency of Protection to create monopolies, of which ample evidence exists in connection with other countries (notably the United States and Germany), will be stronger and still more harmful in a sparsely settled country like South _lfrica." The Chamber even demands the removal of its protective features from the present South African Customs' tariff. Certainly they are not all Protectionists in South Africa. -- " A day of rest" has IF THIS SHOULD been proclaimed by HAPPEN IN IRELAND the Belfast Corporation for "Ulster. Day." Employers are urged to give their employees a holiday—nothing has been said about pay for the compulsory holiday—in order that they may be roped into a "Solemn League and Covenant" against Home Rule. The "Daily Telegraph" correspondent, on the authority of a gentleman "well able to gauge Protestant feeling in Ulster," puts the number of probable signatures at nearly one million out of a total net Protestant population of 430,000. In South Africa, Sir R Baden-Powell declares that Boer and Briton boys throw aside all racial distinction in the" Boy Scout" movement. All are loyal subjects of the British Empire. What a. terrible thing it would seem to the Tory leaders who are encouraging the " Ulster " movement if this should happen in Ireland too!

to the Insurance Act which were paraded on behalf of the Tory Party in Midlothian, that, when the Party's hostility to the Act is not due to pure political bias, it rests upon the deep-rooted prepossession for property. Boteler Grammar School. In the examination, held in July last, for Junior Appointments in the Admiralty, &c., C Haves was placed 53rd and R W Weaver improved on his previous appointment by gaining the 75th place in the same examination. Eighty-one candidates proved successful out of a total number of 298. Mr. G. H. Smith's Marriage.

Mr. George H. Smith, hon. secretary of the Con- servative Association, has been presented by the members with a handsome secretarre and reading lamp in recognition of his recent marriage. Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., made the presentation at a meet- ing held at the club or. Saturday evening under the presidency of Mr. W. W. Westwell. Personal.

A marriage has been arranged between Mr. John Haworth Whitworth, of Church Bank, Bowdon, elder son of the late Mr. John Whitworth, of Manchester, and Ida Mary, only daughter of Mr. Alfred J. King, of Elleray, Windermere. Mr. J. H. Whitworth was the Liberal candidate for the Knuteford division at the general election, and Mr. A. J. King was formerly member for the division.

The Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron, Co., Limited. The directors have decided to recommend the payment of the usual half-year's dividend at the rate of six per cent per annum on both the preference and second preference shares, and a half-year's dividend at the rate of seven per cent per annum on the ordinary shares. They also recommended that the capital expenditure for the year be written off out of profits, that £12,393 be added to the reserve fund, and the balance carried forward to the next account.

Their rendering of the les. pli-ce, selection from " L bengrin," was described by Mr. J. 0. Shepherd, the adjudicator, as great and laultless. Captain A II Spooner, son of Canon Spooner, of Much Woolton, near Liverpool, and brother of ex- Lieutenant R Ii Spooner, the Lancashire County cricketer, has been appointed to the adjutancy of the 2nd Battalion the Lancashire Fusiliers DO.v takiag part in the gzeat Army manoeuvres. The Picturedrome. The enterprising management of the Picturedrome have taken another ppular step by arranging a change of pictures thrice weekly, and its advent this week has clearly been a draw to the many patrons of the Picturedrome. A film depicting the West Lancashire Division of the Territorials in camp at Kirkham has proved exceptionally interesting and the other big attraction has been the film showing the wreck of the Helvetia in mid-ocean. One sees the ' vessel from the collision to total submersion and it is indeed " a marvel of realism." For next week the principal pictures will be :—Monday and Tuesday, "The Sphinx," a story of the French revolution ; Wednesday and Thursday, "The Black Chancellor," a most realistic subject ; Friday and Saturday, When the heart is young." lhe programme will be entirely changed three times.

Death of a Well-known Licensee. A well-known and highly respected townsman has passed away in the person of Mr. 1 hotnas Crompton, the licensee of the Blackburn Arms, Warrington. Although not a native of Warrington,having been born at Lowton in 1856, Mr. Crompton who took over the Blackburn Arms in lBi4, had by his geniality and hearty disposition endeared himself to the large ' number of Warringtonians who enjoyed the privilege of his acquaintance. He was educated at Alston College, near Preston, and was articled to engineering in Keighley. The deceased gentleman had a seizure three years ago and had been in indifferent health since that time He had a further attack on the 3rd inst. from which he never rallied, and his death took place about 9 o'clock on Wednesday night, the cause being hemorrhage of the brain. He leaves a widow and five children,tbree sons and two daughters. Although a Conservative Mr Cronapton never took an active part in political affairs. He was a Churchman and worshipped at Holy Trinity Church. The funeral will take place to-morrow (Sunday) at 3 o'clock at the Cemetery, to be preceded by a service at 9.30 in Holy Trinity Church.

Royal Theatre of Varieties. The Royal stock Company have this week played with pronounced success in the sensational drama " Ile Lady Detective." There are many thrilling situations but there is a good proportion of genuine humour which relieves the heavier aspects of the pro- duction and makes the play most acceptable. The title role is undertaken by Miss Leah Corenters who as Florence Langton, acres a decided success. Mr Harry Val Vousden is again popular as Roderick Tracey, the cool lynx-eyed detective from the Yard. Mr Sam Allen as Barry Mallinson, the man to whom intrigues and crime are as nought, makes the part as loathsome as possible and receives the reward of his efforts—a storm of hisses. As his accomplices Lodovic Stuyvesant and Ph( wbus Rockaway, Mr F Wright and Mr C E Warne are fairly successful, and in an unostentatious way contribute to the comedy of the productioa. Miss Edna Vene plays the part of Ura Langton in an acceptable manner whilst Miss Flo Sransfield is equally successful as Stella Ritzdorf the foil of the scheming Mallinson. Miss Ehie Kerry pleases ;immensely in her catchy songs which she renders in a very acceptable manner.—The Stock Co. will appoar next week in the laughable cyclone' Mc. K,,nnwe Flirtation." div.head: FLOWERY WIDNES.
div.p: FLOWERY WIDNES.

CORPORATION'S EFFORr TO EFFACE A STIGMA The Widnes Market Hall presented an animated appearance on Wednesday evening, the event being an exhibition of plants by the scholars of various schools of the town. The Corporation is trying to encourage plant cultivation among the elementary school children, and the Parks Committee distributed about 900 plants between the children some months ago. There was an excellent attendance, and some 500 plants weve returned on Wednesday. The majority of the plants were in full bloom, and a noticeable exhibit was a large fuoshia which had come from a house in the centre of the manufacturing district. The Mayor (Alderman F Neil), in opAning the exhibition, said the Corporation were hopeful of correcting the description of Widnes. By the means of plant cultivation among the school children they would try to alter the town's desoriptionof "black spot" to a place of "many flowers."

div.head: ARMY VETERAN'S DEATH.
div.p: ARMY VETERAN'S DEATH.
An Indian Mutiny Hero.

Another of the rapidly diminishing band of Indian Mutiny veterans has passed away in the person of Mr. Frederick Wilm- hurst, of 91, Sharp-street who served for over 21 years as a gunner in the Royal Artillery. The deceased, who was in his eighty-third year, was a native of Lewes, Sussex, where he enlisted on March 7th, 1847. He served in China and afterwards passed through some of the most memorable and stirring incidents of the Indian Mutiny. He was present at the Relief of Lucknow, and often recalled the happenings on the march to the beleaguered town, during which the troops underwent great hardships. Mr. Wilmhurst held five good conduct badges and the Indian Mutiny medal with clasps for Lucknow and the Relief of Lucknow. He had lived in Warrington about forty years
NER WILMEIURST,

and was at one time in the employ of the late Mr. Edward Bolton at the glass works in Orftird-lane. He was a man of the highest integrity and took a useful part in religious effo-rt, having for many yrars been identified with the Plymouth Brethren. He was a devout student of the Bible, which he had read through 90 times.

The Mayor (Councillor Dr. Joseph)had long taken a kindly interest in Mr.Wilmhurst and it was largely through his good offices that the deceased was accorded the well-merited honour of a military funeral. An escort and firing party from Orford Barracks were in attendance and at the close of the last rites a volley was fired over the grave and the " Last Post" was sounded. The Mayor was present at the service which was most impressively conducted' on behalf of the Plymouth Brethren, by Mr William Savigar,. of Wigan, Mr James Taylor, of Newton-le- Willows, and Mr J S Percival, of Liverpool.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" Driven from Home."

It is a trihuts to the ennoti,nal power of "Driven from Home " and to the thor, ugh-going manner in which it is acted by Andrew Nleiville's company that the audiences at the R03.a1 Court Theatre this week have been so completely carzied away as to be unable to repress their feelings. The villain, who does nothing by halves, has had a ptiticularly warm time, popular loathing of his misdeeds having been trans- late•B' into loud " booing " and uncomplimentary 1, interjecti ins. But this, from the villain's point of view, is just as it should be. The, how the "gods " have exclaimed with anguish when the frail. innocent foundling boy has been p!aced on tie circular saw, and how they have cheered to the echo the arrival, im the nick oz time, of the rescuer. It is all very thrilling and the con- densation of the play,.to.bring it within the compass of two shows nightly, ensures an utibrokn su-cession of action and incident, without a m meat of dullness. Mr George Mitchell gives a striking portrayal of Anthony Ray hi °oh, the stern father %nose cruel treat- ment of his daughter breaks his proud spirit and brings him nothing but iernora-i. His acting is natural and convincing. Miss Eva Norman enlists the sympathies of the audience as L tura I?aybrook, the daughter who is turned adrift to perisn, and fully realises the contrast between the bright winsome girl, surrounded by luxury, in the first act, and the pitiable outcast whom starvation ultimately claims as a victim. Mr Phil Harper as Geoffrey Waring, the villain of the play, gives a most effective study of an unpalatable part and deserves much of the credit for the intensity with which the p ay grips the audience. He is a villain of the cool, smooth-tongued, calculating order, and das his work really well. Mr Henry Scatcharci as Dick S zunders is a typical accomplice —mercenary and audacious. Much-a ppre- ciated comic relief is provided by Mr Fred C Imbert and Miss Dora Hargreaves as John Anderson and his wife. The play is well-aramted in a dozen scenes and the orchestrs under 'Ur Baathr..3d's c,uductorship plays some capital selections.

div.head: OPEN-AIR POLITICS.
div.p: OPEN-AIR POLITICS.
MR. HAROLD SMITH'S ATTACK ON THE PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.
Spirited Rejoinder.

The Warrington Progressive Labour League brought its summer campaign at Bridge Foot to a close on Monday evening when another largely attended and enthusiastic meeting was held. Mr. J. El well presided and the principal speaker was Mr. T. M. Evans, of Liverpool. The bitter attack made upon the League by Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., at the Tory open-air meeting on Saturday evening, called forth a spirited rejoinder. fhe CHAIRMAN slid be was greatly amused on read- ing in the Press last week of an exciting scene in the Town Council, during which an Aldermaadescrihed the Insurance Act as" the greatest swindle of the century," aud in the nest sentence said he knew nothing about it. (Laughter.) That, be submitted, was typical of the great majority of Tories. When they came to look at a great Liberal measure' they declared it to be no good before they had studied it to find whether there was any good in it or not. He (the speaker) listened ta _

div.head: MR. HAROLD SMITet
div.p: MR. HAROLD SMITet

on Saturday night and heard- him Cleclare that he was in favour of the principle of the Insurance Act, but that the Government ought to have appealed to the people before placing it on the Statute Book. Let them hare beak to the time whei the Conserva- tives were in power. Did they consult the people before passing their Education Bill ? No.") They were returned to power to finish the work they had begun in South Africa. He (the speaker) knew of many good Liberals in Warrington who voted Con- servative because they said the Conservatives had got into a holeand the best course %vas to leave them to get out of it. The Conservatives extricated themselves from their difficulties by piling debt upon debt, leaving the Liberals to clear thew off when they succeeded to office. The Liberals not only took over the burden and greatly reduced the national debt, but they had paid tneir own way as they west along. (Applause.) In almost every Conservative paper they were told that the Liberals promised the °neap loaf. They did not promise that, but they promised that the loaf should not be made any d-arsr through artificial restrictions (Hear, hear.) What they contended was that to place a tariff upon bread must of necessity make it dearer. Conservatives were also fond of asking where was the great increase of trade which the Liberals predicted ? They had only to look at the monthly returns of the Board of Trace to see the vast expansion that ass taking place month after mouth and year alter year. The increase applied not only to quantities but to values. The workman was getting higter was for he labour and as a natural result tan shop keeper got higher prices for the articles he sold. They wanted the national prosperity to be shared all round, and he con- tended that the policy adopted in this country sixty years ago had been the most beneficent one that it was possible to take up. The people of this country were more contented than those of any other country. The Conservative party pointed to strikes as being symptomatic of discontent and unrest. When did men striae ? Wnen there was uo trade ? No. They , knew that if they went ou strike at a time of trade depression the employer could close his works for a month or two. It was when there was plenty of trade and the men saw there was an opportunity of attaining something, that they went on etrike. In connection with his own trade, there never was a time in the history of this country when the prospects were brighter than at present. (Applause.) The Conservative policy, he maintained. would tend to foster industries which were not congenial to the country and in which the wages were comparatively low, at the expense of the more highly-paid trades. (Applause). Mr Eva.ss said the by-elections at Crewe and North- West Manchester were said to indicate that the electors had lost confidence in the Liberals and that they were only awaiting the opportunity of a general election in order ignominously to dismisss a Government of hum- bugs, to adopt the language of Mr F E Smith, and to put in their place the wild beast of Toryism (Laughter.) The acclaiming of those results by the Tory party was a ridiculous, ludicrous and pitiable pretence. Crewe and North-West Manchester were not going to cause the slightest perturbation in the orbit of the new Liberalism. Whatever temporary reverses the Government might suffer, there would he "no variableness nor shadow of turning" on their part, from the road on which they bad set out. (Applause.) Liberals were imbued with that spirit which meant that when they fell they simply rose again ; when they were defeated it was only that they might fight the better. (Applause.) There was an old saying that drowning men clutched at straws, and that was appar- ently the position of the Tories with regard to the by-elections. (Hear ,hear.) Had they forgotten West Norfolk, Hanle3,Holmflrth and Carmarthen ?(Applause.) Surely the result of Carmarthen alone muat have done something to chasten the transports of their opponents. Alluding to Mr. Harold Smith's objection that the Insurance Act had been rushed through the House of Commons, the speaker pointed out that it engaged the attention of the House for 65 days—longer taan was devoted to any single piece of legislation since the beginning of the nineteenth century, not excepting the great Reform Act of 1332. The plea that more time should have been spent on the measure was all

FUDGE AND BUNKUM and a mere excuse. Mr. Bonar Law was asked to state, in the event of the Tory party being returned to power within the nest twelve months, what amendments they would propose to the Insurance Act, to bring it more into line with popular favour. That was a simple, straightforward question. Did he give a straightfor- ward answer ? Not a bit of it. Mr. B mar Law's reply was to this effect : "It is impossible for me to indicate what amendments we shall move to the Insur- ance Act, while in opposition, but we shall drastically amend it." If the Tories were sincere they could, with- out giving the show away, indicate the broad lines on which their amendments would go. They had now almost exhausted the capital they could make out of the Insurance Act. From January onwards, when the people realized some of its benefits, the Act would pass from the debit to the credit side of popular favour. (Applause). With regard t Home Rule, the speaker said the leaders of Toryisru, big and little were, peats ing the

div.head: NEW ANARCHY
div.p: NEW ANARCHY

in the language of the new style. They were prepared to form a provisional Government against, the lawfully established Constitution of the country. They were even prepared to head revolutions, to lead the forces of sectarian bigotry and racial animosity against the new laws, and now they were talking of impeaching the Prime Minister. (Laughter.) What balderdash and bitukum ! When the beads of the Tory party avowed themselves the leaders and champions of irresponsible , and swaggering rowdies, they were taking over a very grave responsibility. The Ulster Tories bud turned a complete political somersault. One moment they declared that they would not be put outside the Constitution wnich they claimed as their birthright, and the next they were going to ignore that constitution and set up a provisional Government. If Ulster was determined to traverse the road of treason- dble conspiracy, who was going to be the President of the new Republic? Somebody might suggest Mr Row Law, but he could not be rpared—he was too valuable an asset to the Liberal party.

div.head: WHAT ABOUT ME. F. E. SMITH?
div.p: WHAT ABOUT ME. F. E. SMITH?

Oh, no, he was to be the future Premier of the Imperial Parliament at Westminster and he was far too smart and shrewd a man to exchange the Premiership for the doubtful honour of the Crown of Ulster. (Laughter.) By a process of exclusion and elimination, they arrived at one other name—Sir Edward Carson. The finger of fate seemed to point to him as the heavy villain of the piece. (Laughter.) No douht he would be weighted with that crown, and they would wish him happiness in the wearing of it, at ths same time reminding him of the saying "Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown" and he had better beware lest the modern Sir Galahad ended his days in the Tower of L mdon, as the hero of comic opera. (Laughter. Let the Cecils, the Smiths, the Londonderries and the Carsocs stand aside and nothing would happen in Ulster which would be discreditable to that province. (Applause.) There was an increasing number of Protestants in Ulster, as well as in other parts of Ireland, who were not only prepared to accept but heartily to welcome the just, sound, financial measure of self-government which the Imperial Parlia- ment offered to that country. Alluding to Tariff Reform, the speaker said the Tories put it out of sight in North-West Manchester and trampled it under foot. They showed a desire to fight in any issue save Tariff Reform. lie noticed that the Warrington tarifiiits had generated sufficient courage to hold a

div.head: JOY DAY AT NEW BRIGHTON.
div.p: JOY DAY AT NEW BRIGHTON.

(Laughter.) They assembled, to the wonder and amaze- ment of Liverpool, on the plateau at Sr.. George's Hall with" our member "at t3eir head. (Laughter.) They were quite right when they said " Our member." (A VOICE : "Only women.") "He certainly is not your choice" commented Mr. Evans ^ and be certainly would not be mine, so they are perfectly welcome to designate him 'our member.' 1 hope they will not be able to say our member ' after the next election, but 'our pet.'" (Laughter.) The speaker expressed regret at the apparently widening breach. between the forces of organiz.d Labour and Liberalism and said no true friend of the workers, who was whole-heal ted in his desire for social amelioration, could view it with any- thing but grave misgiving and concern. They were faced by the
- HYDRA-lIEADED MONSTER OF REVOLUTIONARY SOCIALISM.

He did not say ordinary Socialism, bu'-• revolutionary Socialism and Syudio,lism which seemed to have cap- tured the Labour Party in this country. He did not hesitate to say, whether his hearers agreed with him or not, that the revolutionary Socialist and the Syndi- calist was a standing menace to progressive and con- tinued advance in the days which were immediately before them. (Hear, hear.) Having referred to the demo- cratic legislation enacted under the regime of the pre- sent Government, the speaker contended that it would

be suicidal for the two wings of the progressive force to indulge in internal welfare at this juncture, as it would cripple the effectiveness of both sections, and the wild beast of Toryism was standing by, waiting to devour the spoils. He welcomed the growth of organized labour and the spread of His trade union spirt, and he was prepared to see a much larger numerical representation of Labour in the House of Commons. But he wanted that increased representation to be won, not at the expense of their allies in the march of progresm. but at the expense of the powers of privilege and monopoly. (Applause.) He wanted Liberalism and Labour to unite,band in hand, in comhat against the remnants of feudalism in this county. (Applause). Mr E.WYNNE JONEi said that on Saturday Warrington was honoured with a visit from " our member " who, he was told,barl something to say about the Progressive& Labour League. It was clear that the work which the League was cirrying on bad

UPSET MR. SMITH a little bit. (Hear, hear.) He understood Mr Smith told his audience that the League was a farce—that it was simply a wing of the Liberalsparty. In so fer tlakt in the past they had supported a Liberal cat:initiate. for the borough. that efts absolutely true. He would tell them the exact position of the League : They were progressives cud social ref ortuers but they believed the best way to get social reform was by evolution and not by revolution. They were something like Oliver Twist—they were prepared to take anything they could get, provided it was reform, and then its for more. That was the sensible poaition which every reformer had to take up. They bad in the past supported a Liberal candidate find he would like to tell Mr. Smith that in future they would support a progressive candidate and se that Mr. Smith was turne4 out. (Applause. Mr. Smith further alleged that he could count the members of the Leaaue on the fingers of both hands. All he could say was that Mr Smith must have very big hands, if that were the case. (Lnughter).The membership of that L.taelle was some- thing like 700. and with the exneptiou t f about a dozen, all bad votes. (Applausa.) The battalion that Mr. Smith led down Dale-street last Thursday had not got a single vote. (Laughter.) He hoped the members of the League would take u? that insult of Mr. Smith's when- the next fight came. (Hear, hear). Mr. Smith also had something to say about the gentlemen who had honoured the League with visits from time to time. He was said to have described them as "imported hirel ngs, brought here to abuse the Member." It was his (Mr. Jones's) experience that those people who abused most were the most ready to complain when they happened to be hit back, and that was exactly the position ot Mr Harold Smith. He must have forgotten himself entirely when he talked about hirelings. He must have been thinking about the tariff reform lecturers who came there from time to time. To apply such a term as "imported hire- ling" to their friend who had addressed them thatzlight was an absolute insult. He (the speaker) supposed Mr Smith was hard up for something to say and that was the best thing that came to him, or perhaps he was intoxicated with a little succass, after leading that splendid battalion to New Brighton. (Laughter.) If any man was under

PETTICOAT GOVERNMENT that man was Harold Smith, for when the men went to New Brighton he was able to send a letter of apology, hut last Thursday he had to toe the line and turn up. ( Laughter.) The Tories talked about the Liberals having to too the line to John Redmond but Mr. Smith had to toe the line to the Women's Tariff Reform League, or his political life would soon be at an end. They did not mind a single bit what Mr. Smith bad to say about the Progressive Labour League. All they could do to Fee that the borough was represented by a thorough democrat would be done by the League.

When the next fight came he did not think there was t soy doubt that toe gentletuan who did not represent in a proper way the constituency at the present time would be turned out. (Applause.) The Tory party were very mad because Mr. Lloyd George was going to start a great campaign on the land question. They knew that when that question was tackled, it would be good-bye to Tory government for many a long day. Monopoly in land was going to be broken down, and the finest leader they could have in a campaign like that was that great and thorough demo- crat—the finest democrat who ever sat in the House of Commons, Mr. Lloyd George. (Applause.) By just and fair legislation the land could be opened up for the people and not kept in the hands of the few. Mr Harold smith said the Progressive Labour League was only part and parcel of the Liberal Party. He (the speaker) was not ashamed of that, if the Liberal party stood for things that were good, but the Labour League had had a separate programme for years, apart from the Liberal party, end a drastic reform of the land laws had been part of it. They wanted to see a readjustment not only of imperial but of local taxation and the atolition of the present land system under which they had the idle rich at one end of society and the workless poor at the other. They also stood for a complete reform of the iniquitous Poor Law and they believed the Insurance Act would prove to be one step in that direction, by setting up a great barrier between the poor and the Workhouse. (Applause). Mr E JAMES, in seconding a vote of thanks to the speaker. said tuat at New Brighton toe Member had somethiog to say about the Women's Liberal Associa- tion. All he (the speaker) could say was that Mr Smith must have a tremendous pocket if, as he said, be could put the Women's Liberal Association into it. (Laughter.) His pocket must have got larger since he came to. Warrington, for several reasons. He (the speaker) could not help being struck with the ingratitude of Mr Smith. The Government had been kind enough to put £4OO a year into his pocket, but he was not at all thankful to them. (Laughter.) The Women's Ltherni Association took a prominent-. part in securing the return of Mr Crosfield at two successive elections and he (the speaker) believed they would work with equally good results at the next election. (Applause.)

div.head: CRUSHED BY A WAGGON.
div.p: CRUSHED BY A WAGGON.
Mr. Brighouse held an inquiry, at Widnes, into the circumstances attending the death of Samuel Glassey, a chemical labourer,who was haled at Pilking- ton'a works on September 4th. _ . _

John Jackson, iorreman labourer, said that he ordered nine men to move a waggon from a turntable to an unloading shed. Glassey and witness went in front of the waggon, and the others pushed behind. Once inside the shed the waggon had a clearance on one side of 2 ieet 3 inches, and on the other of 3 inches only. On the narrow side was situated the brake, aria it was here that Glassey was killed. Witness aid not know if Glassey went to the brake, but he was terribly crushed between the waggon and a brick column and the 3 inch space side. In answer to the Coroner, witness said there was no necessity to touch the brakes wben once the waggon was in the shed, and there was no necessity for him to have been in front. _

The Coroner suggested that the brake should be on the wider side. Witness said there was not suf:Mient room to turn the waggon round. Tneojury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and recommended thst alterations should oe made to turn the Ytagguns round so that the brake would always be on the wider side.
