Several of the Posts have mused upon :he Severn's waters, none more touchingly than Tennyson, who, in hi tribute in the "In Memo- •iam" to Arthur Hallam, thus alludes to his friend's resting place: "The Danube to the Severn gave The darkeu'd heart that beat no more; They laid him by the pleasant shore, And in the hearing of the wave."

Of the charms of the Avon family of rivers; the Upper or Warwieksaire Avon, the Lower or Bristol Avon, and the East Avon, every peths- rian bears testi-mony whose privileged foot- steps have wandered amidst their several wind- ing ways.

div.head: [COPYRIGHT.]
div.p: [COPYRIGHT.]
ENGLISH RIVER HIGHWAYS.
PUBLISHED BY SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT.

Probably no country in the world has rivers of more charm or greater sea-borne traffic thar those of old England. Whethei one takes intc account the rivers of longer course, which empty themselves into the North Sea, or those, shorter in length, on the west coast, with the exception of the Severn, they present both picturesque attractionp and immense variety of shipping. Famous in song and story, they make appeal to every class of Englishman. Such waterways as the Tyne, Tees, Wear, Humber, Mersey, Severn, and Thames, sur- rounded with innumerable associations, bind Great Britain with every quarter of the globe.

div.head: " COALY TYNE."
div.p: THE " COALY TYNE."

In many respects "Coaly Tyne" has unique features. Its high banks guarding, as it were, much of its course, ite numerous industries and turbid waters on the lower reaches, sug- gist comparisons alone with the Clyde at Glas- gow. Some 20,000 veseels use the port annually, the largest ea-craft being accommodated at ,the quay, the great terminus of the port's river traffic. Flowing through the richest coal-min- ing region of Britain, the waters of the Tyne join the sea between Tynemouth and South Shields, the entrance to which in North Sea gales is more dreaded by captains than the mouth of any other river on British shores. In a graphic pen picture of the Port of the''fyne, 'Clark Russell says: "I know no spectacle in its way more stirring and impreesive than the -scene of the Liver Tyne as surveyed from the High Level Bridge. From the altitude of the .greatcst monument of engineering skill and strength anywhere to be found, with locomo- tives dragging their rattling and echoing trains high above your head, you look down upon an incomparable picture of human life. . . It is % scene one could stand and look down on for 'hours. There is no magic in ink and but little 7ven in pigments, I should think—to give colour to it, to reproduce the life, the energy, the sug- gestions of wealth, the labour, the triumphant resolution of it. You feel as you gaze that hie people Who have never seen the Tyne and 1170/icier at the Newcastle man's honest en- thusiasm when it is mentioned, ouzht to be at votir side looking down, too." Other North of England rivers of note embrace the Tees, navigable in recent times for vessels of large burden, as far as Stockton, and the Wear, at whose 'mouth .Surderland stands. represented f)V large iron ship-building yards, end some hogs- docks, from which enormous shipments 3f coal and coke are annually made.

div.head: WORLD'S GREATEST PORT.
div.p: THE WORLD'S GREATEST PORT.

On the north-western coast of England, the litersey commands universal interest by the liversity of its shipping, linking the city of ...Averpool with the whole civilised world. What :his indicates may be inferred from figures show- ng that Liverpool now conducts one-third of he export trade and one-fourth of the import :rade of the United Kingdom, besides owning me-third-of the total shipping of the kingdom, Ind one-seventh of the total registered shipping )f the globe; to the handling of which it is esti- mated that about 1,1C0,000 souls are largely de- mmdent noon the port for a livelihood. Oppo- site the city, the 3fers?y is a mile and a quarter n breadth, with a sufficient depth of sea-room it low water to allow the greatest vessels to ipproaeh the pier. The estuary is obstructed 'corn sandbanks, but its excellent body of )ilots, admirably constructed sea-walls, and =ystem of dredging in order to keep the !hamlet of the river clear for the pas- ;age of gigantic ships, not only com- iine to render navigation comparatively ;ate, but also to give it one of the toblest of harbours. Sailing into the Mersey 'rem the sea on a summer's day, the panorama Teens on the river, the varied shippinc, monster locks—triumpbe of engineering skill, together with a view of the city's buildings, form one )f the world's most fascinating pictures of marl_ time enterprise.

div.head: ENGLAND AND THE CONTINENT.
div.p: ENGLAND AND THE CONTINENT.

Turning eastwards again, the waterway of the Efumber offers a distinct contrast to that of the stereey. Comprising the rivers Ouse and Trent, :he Humber flows through some of England's nost beautiful scenery, intermingled with •omantio and historical associations. Among tg outstanding characteristics one learns that 't has the largest drainage basin of any Eng- ish river, covering an area of 9,550 square Ili-1M i.e., about one-sixth of the entire sonntry, while by navigable streams and canals :he Humber is connected across England with :he Mersey, Severn, and Thames. By way of :he Humber, say the 'historians, came the old 3anish war-vessels, happily supplanted in n'fldern times by peaceful craft on the Ilfum- bees broad waters bearing well-nigh endless !argoes of niineralts and woollen goods from the )ort of Hull to the most distant shores. On the I.outh bank of the Humber the fishing port of 3rimsby has a world-wide name by its extensive freights of fish, its quays always affording ,pidies in marine denizens and strange visitors from the deep.

div.head: TH WINDING SEVERN.
div.p: TH WINDING SEVERN.

The Severn, one of Dnglaml's Most delightful nd important river highways, with outlet in ;he Bristol Channel, makes strong appeal to the magination by its extraordinary zig-zag pas- sage seawards. What this implies may be in- 'erred from the circumstance that its course of :10 miles, from F,ource to mouth, only repre- sents ‘`243 miles aa the crow flies. One of it chief

div.head: "THE ROYAL RIVER."
div.p: "THE ROYAL RIVER."

What volumes of lore might be penned con- cerning Father Thames, which, like all jive's, L an endless allegory of the fate of men and nations. No river in the world has a tithe of its literary, artistic. historical, and sea-faring memories. "Sweet Thames, run softly till I end my song," wrote Spenser; and the river ever since has been running to an accom- paniment of praise. Drayton and Pope have pourtrayed it in daintiest word-pictures, and most of all Denham—whose rhythmic lines are known to every schoolboy:
"Though deep yet clear, though gentle yet not
„ dull, strong withent rage, without overflowing„ full.”

In what pomp of -colour, too, Turner immor- talised the Thames on canvas, just as in more recent times Vicat Cole's "Pool of London" has had powerful charm . Few men are possibly familiar with the en- tire course of "The Royal River," and none can know it co well as frequenters of its various sections. Dickens, for example, Was as inti- mate with the river near town, and below, about Gravesend and near the Medway, as Matthew Arnold with the upper waters, or as the London boating man in general with Mar- low and Henley. Far in the slopes of the Cotswold Hills it takes rise, clear and pure, en- joying a bright and swift life among sleepy villages, and beneath vernal woods, before it goes into business, so to speak, near Oxford, and becomes a kind of as- sistant drainage commissioner to. various owns. Coal barges float on it, commerce creeps up this silent and now rather dirty highway, and, finally, the stream reaches London, goes into the City. and Dlil3'6 the Dart of a wide water-street, along which by bridge, rail, or boat, countless thousands of souls pass daily. "No- where does it quite lose its beauty," observes a writer, "however man may deface and defile it, Pollutehr as it is by human dirt, and ignorance, and waste, checked by stone embankments, and bridled with bridges, the river retains the force and 601 TIC, of the beauty of a natural power." Even the sea ,wind seems to blow an along its current from the sea, while the waters we gaze upon at the Temple stairs have come from the very heart of England, and carry memories V hills, and meadows, and water,weeds. Wonderfully entrancing is the " Historic Thames," from its course round about Oxford, redolent of clustriad poplars and the old red roofs of waterside houses. until one looks upon its mighty waters with the moving of st%imers in Tilbury Docks, and the incessant passing to and fro of raft of every shape and size, ere it passes to (hr grey vast reaches between Gravesnil and the ore, in happy old age, to its holm, in the sea.

div.head: WOMAN'S TELL-TALE EYES.
div.p: WOMAN'S TELL-TALE EYES.

One need not be a very keen student to read the secrets disclosed by a woman's eyes. They are the lamps of the soul, the rnesseng-rs of joy or grief with- in Too often they tell of pain that is being borne in secret, of a dread that is never quite at rest—the dread of coming pain. Looking at these honest and often beautiful eyes one longs to tell the owners that the secret pain which they betray, the fear of which they are haunted, might be avoided. Thousands of women —some of them little more than girls —are suffering unnecessary pain because they know of no remedy. Time and time again there comes to them a dull ache in the back, pains in both sides, and a dreadful feeling of depression and weakness. In many cases they are completely prostrated, and find themselves unable to go through the day's routine. One of the greatest martyrs to these ailments of women was a Derbyshire lady, whose experience has come to our knowledge. She cured herself by a very simple remedy. In a letter she writes :—" I feel it my bounden duty to send a few lines Raving suffered for many years, and got no relief from any- thing, I at last took my husband's advice and purchased , a 2s. N. bottle of Lydia E. Pirikham's Vegetable I Compound. After two doses I was surprised at the relief I had got, and now, after taking a few bott!es I feet greatly benefited, and can say that the pain I used to experience has entirely left me. I am per- fectly convinced that I owe my relief to your wonder- ful Vegetable Compound." All women who suffer like this lady should write for the remedy which cured her. Any chemist will supply it at .2s. 9d. a bottle, or 4s. 6d. for a very latge bottle. The Lady Manager, c/o The Lydia E. div.p: THE WEER END SPORT.

USELESS LIKE FLIES. MR. JOSEPH FELS ON LANDLESS AIEIC. Mr. Joseph Fels, speaking at Whitefield's Tabernacle, on Sunday afternoon, said that until they settled the land question they were ju, t like flies in the springtime absolutely useless and entirely unable to do anything else except worship the rich and tare the droppings from their tables. Until they could "choke off " tho Speculator in hied values they would continue to be slaves. The London County Council, continued the speaker, had stated that there were no fewer than 14,0'..0 acres; of unused land within the metropolis. If each man had but an eighth of an acre upon which to grow food for his family there would be 123,000 more gardens than there are now, each owned probably by the head of a family. If this land were by some hocus-pocus forced into use there would not be an idle man in London, unless he wanted to be, nor would there be a hungry man or a man or woman ashamed to go into the streets for want of good clothes.

gracious spirit of their forerunners, to remind themselves again of the religious ideals for which they stood and of the obligations they were uader. Ile desired to call to their minds once again the great, all-inclusive ideal of religion and of the religions iife for which that chapel and all its kindred chapels s-mod. The deepest essence of religion was unspeak- able; It could not be stated in any set of formulas, it Doubt never be compressed into a creed or dogma to which adherence should he demanded as a condition of salvation. The religion of the Clatireh Universal was wholly of the spirit, its gospel was of the spirit, a whispering of the eternal through the hails of time, to be received and comprehended by the heart, to be realised in loyalty and love. Toe forms of that gospel might and did change from ago to age, but its essence remained the same eiernally. Those who felt its influence became indeed members one of another and could no longer endure the separating barriers of hunan and fallible intellectual distinctiona. The law of that Church of the Living God, so founded and established in spiritual religion, was the law of liberty. " The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." The law of liberty was neither the permission of licence nor the anarchy of mere subjective freedom. There was no question there of freedom to di or to say simply what pleased one at the moment. The law of lil-erty bound a man's spirit in a loyal enslavement to God which permitted no liberty outside the right and the good and allowed no freedom except that of self-abludonment in the finite world and self-recovery in the eternal world of God's Kingdom. rhe liberty of the spirit left free a man's intellect to.. search and consider and inquire, taking no merely finite virwof truth as final and secure but it fettered his soul in bonds of devotion to truth itself and of loyalty and love to the eternal order. The Church of the Living God would bear no sectarian sectionalizing name. Bread-based upon the rock of the Spirit, its love would he so w!clfs as to include all differences of theological .opinion, and in that way, though it would be passing rich in doctrines, in beliefs which men hold honestly and sincerely, It would be without dogma, recognizing no external authority as sufficient to hamper true freedom, but relying solely upon the spiritual authority of love and service:as equal to the controlling of all base particularity,and the avoidance of all bitterness where differences occurred. It would accept from the past all that growing experi- ence found valuable in the way of doctrine, institution and symbol, but it would not limit Itself to any par- ticular formalism or seek to impose on its members

any needless ritual or doubtful article of belief. In its activity it would b-t essentially redemptive and in a secondary deg-ee social, holding fast the ideal of a per- fected humanity irk Christ and working from the rule of self-sacrificing service the law of its freedom. Against every social ill and secret wrong it would speak through its minister and people, with no hesitating voice, founding its aut,hority not in the temporal powers and rulera of this world, but in the pure end holy justice, the Divine and gracious love of God's Kingoom.

div.head: Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.
div.p: Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay.

- This (Saturday) afternoon the handsome and well- appointed new vestry at the Workingmen's Mission, Bank Qatty will be opened by Mrs. John Crostield, Colwyn Bay. The building which will accommodate about 140 adults, has been erected by Messrs. C. W. Davenport and Sons, Stockton Heath, to the d esign of Mr. S. P. Silc Warrington. 'fbe entire cost of vestry and furniture (about iC.O3) has been defrayed by Mrs. John Crusfield, the object being to provide additional accommodation for Sunday Scholl work. Among those will ail' take part in to-day's ceremony are the Revs. John Yonge and W. Reid and Councillor R. Henshall.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

Preaching on Sunday morning at St John's, Rev W Reiu said that the early Puritans, imperfect apart from those who were to follow, built better than they knew, making possible the larger Puritanism. While the unjustifitble features, in themselves temporary, had dropped away, the principle of their life remained unc.tanged, and to-day as then, found its true expres- sion in simplicity, duty, and continued sense of Ciud's presence. In the evening Mr Reid traced the movemen towards freedom in the Church from the pre-Reforma- tion days of Wyclif, through the days of trie Tud,..r and Stuart times, until the great Ejectment of 1662 Deploring what had come to be a nation's loss, despi e ninny games accruing therefrom, and acknowledging the impossibility of any backward movement, be said the tutute was with sat and the inevitable evolution of the best in every hrancl of the Caristiaa Caurch, must us ineviLably result in re-union.

div.head: " The Ideal of a Free Church."
div.p: " The Ideal of a Free Church."

The Rev Dr Stanley A Mellor preached at Cairo- street chapel on Sunday eveniug on "The ideal of a Free Church." His text was "Ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem and in all Judm t. and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost parts of the earth " (Acts i. 8). He said that that nay, with a concord and unanimity altogether desirable though infrequently Achieved, the Nonconformist chapels of the teat] were engaged in celebrating the 2:.,0,h anniversary et an event in the religious life of Englsnd which, in importance and tar-reaching significance, was to be comparad only with the Reforma- tion which severed the Church in England from its Catholic ancestry. By them in that particular chapel, the ejectment of 2,00 clergy in 1662 was, or should he, a matter of perpetual remembrance. That chapel, alone of the Noncoutormist places of worship in Warrington, originated directly from the days of tbe ejection ; the first minister of that place was one Rouert Yates, previously Rector of the Warrington Parish Church, drivel!' from his living because be felt himself unable to subscribe to the provisions of the Act of Uniformity, because he would not endanger his freedom. They stretched back over those no years with an unbroken line of tradition, and It was, he believed, no unjustifiable boast to declare that,during all the varying chances and changes of those long years, that chapel had remained superbly lotal to its fundamental principle of freedom in religion. It was established by men who sought to unburden them- selves of hampering fetters. by men who dedicated themselves and their Church to the free worship of Almighty God, and never, front that hour, had any attempt Peen made to impose on ministers or rnembers in that place a religions or rather theological test of any kind. Opinions and doctrines had changed, time arid again, with the years, but never once had sub- scription to a creed or a dogma been demanded or expected. Where were their articles of faith to which they set their mark ? They did not exist. Where was the statement of belief which should serve as test of their fitness for the ministry or the membership of that chapel? It was not to he found. Freely they entered and freely they abodi together: in friedorn they spose the word that was in their hearts, in freedom they lifted their hand in prayer to heaven, seeking always and only to be the serverits of the spirit and never the slaves of the letter. But it was not theirs to boast ; the glory was of God arid not of themeelves, nor did they begin again to commend themselves Rather they would humbly Dee that occasion, remembering the noble history of bygone years, the fine romance of that great adventure, the

div.head: Primitive Methodist Church, Legh-street.
div.p: Primitive Methodist Church, Legh-street.

An interesting series of reunion services took place at this church ors Sund.y and Monday when many past and present workers met to renew acquaintanceship. Efforts had been made to trace all who had been con- nected*with the church in years gune by and invitations were issued to as many as could he discovered. The preacher for the day was the Rev J B Bugloss who has seen two terms of service on the Warrington circuit Over forty years ago he came here as a prohationcr and laboured very acceptably for three years. Six years ago he returned to the original scene of his labours and spent another profitable three years as superintendent. On Sunday afternoon eraversl speakers reviewed the work of the ' church in the part and spoke hopefully of the future. Mr. J. Griffiths presided and the choir rendered special anthems. Among those who paid return visits to the church may be mentioned Mrs. Vrigit, from New Z..,ts- bind, and Mrs. Finch, widow of the late Rev. Charles Finch, a former minister at Legh-street. Letters of appreciation were received from America, Africa and New Zealand. On Monday evening, under the chair- manship of Mr. Richard Bridge, the Rev. J. B. Bugloss lectured on " The relationship of sciencetto faith.' In view of recent declarations made in the British Associ- ation meetings, his utterances were specially appreci- ated. Mr. Buglass is a robust thinker and to him: Christianity receives stimulation and verification from science. The whole of the gatherings were greltly enjoyed end hopes are entertained that similar re-unions will be promoted.

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church.
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church.

The Rev. G. E. Cheeseman, of Huyton Congregational Church pret.ched morning and evening at Wyetiff-. Church, on Sunday. In an address to the children he told an interesting story of the shadow of Christ and pointed a useful moral. His sermon was based on the text " For we walk by faith and not by sight." (11. Cur. sc. 7v). It did net matter whether a man was a Christian or en unbeliever, be said, the text was still a truth. An unbeliever bad to take every step in the journey of life by faith. A man must believe in some- thing or he would do nothing. Faith was the inspira- tion of action. It was men of faith who had been pioneers in the world's progress. The preacher pro- ceeded to show how in business and iu social life faith in one another was essential. It was the boast of science that she did all her work by sight and never took anything on tru-r. lie did not know bow many had read Profersor Schafer's address to the British Association last week but running through the whple of I that address were various assemptions—the imaginings ,of a man's mind. Every great discovery of science had Faith hilt was of been the outcome of inissination and y hat some people sciamlipedlyimsapr giiintaut,,ilonimthieeißoailt)Leuhcalsiecdienfeee as faith. F faith—faith in the uniformity of nature, faith that the laws of nature would never be broken. What were the ! laws of nature ? They wore only the wa3s God worked. The laws themselves aj no power ; laws could not do , anything. There were laws on the statute book against theft, but they did not prevent felony. It was the power behind the laws which men dreaded The laws of nature had no power in themselves. It was "necause there was a great Law Giver behind the laws. Without Hind at the heart of the universe there would Ibe no order and no law. If it were not for faith in the uniformity of nature the chemist might abandon his laboratory and the scientist might give up his researches The faith which reposed in man was bound up with faith in God, and the moment a man lost faith in God he began to lose faith in man. Though Profeisor Schafer looked forward to the time when matter would spontaneously produce life,he bad to admit that life had always been the creation of life, and that admission destroyed the whole force of his address. At the evening service Mr. Che semen based his remarks on the text " I find no fault itr Him " (John xix. 6). That was the verdict of Pilate, he said, con- cerning Christ. The life of Jesus had been before the world for twenty centuries and in every age there had been people who had had the avowed intention of find- ing fault, but their verdict was that of Pilate. The preacher quoted the results of the analyses of Christ's character by John Stuart Mill and Professor L.ckv. Christ's life was one to he copied and he urged his hearers to learn the art of Christian living.

div.head: Warrington and District Baptist Union.
div.p: Warrington and District Baptist Union.

The annual meetings of the above union were held on Thursday at the historic old church at Hill Cliffe, when a large company of local Baptists gathered together, the Lancashire iin the meeting being of a very happy and successful nature. The gatherings were honoured by the presence of Rev .1 Moffatt Logan of Accrington, Moderator of h sermon o n ndC ht the A the afternoon service, and preached an impressive and inspiring thy sins be forgiven thee." Following this service tea seh wordass, o, c Son, Association, who of good cheer,, who conducted was served in the adjoit ing school/rerun, this being followed by a public meeting, presided over by Rev J S Chedburn, in the absence of M W H Bradford, president. After the meeting had been opened by singing and prayer, the chairman publicly welcomed the pastor and delegates of the Widnes Church, who attended the meetings of the union for the first time. Rev G Pope of Liverpool, was then called upon to address the meeting, end responding, gave an address which touched the hearts of his bearers as he appealed for their increased loyalty and devotion to the work 'for which the Church exists. At a later point of the meeting the Rev Alexander Harvey, Widnes, delivered an address which was an earnest appeal for the pre-eminence of Jesus Christ , amongst his followers. He urged His absolute pre- eminence as a man amongst men; as a teacher amongst the world's teachers; and whilst teachers of other religions had each some measure of truth,He tmoscended them all by teaching all truth ; as Saviour Ile was pre- eminent in that. He came to save and to seek only that which was lost; and lastly be claimed for Jesus Christ, pre-eminence as Lord and Master and urged more com- plete and whole hearted obedience to His demands for service. During the evening meeting the anthems
“Pray for the peace of Jerusalem,” and As tbs bseo'j. pantetb." were tastefully sung hy the choir, 191' Atli! being taken by Mrs Kenworthy, whilst Abss Grounds accompanied on the organ.

div.head: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON NONCONFORMITY.
ITS 250th ANNIVERSARY

div.head: Declaration of Indulgence and the First Nonconformist Meeting Place.
div.p: The Declaration of Indulgence and the First Nonconformist Meeting Place.

Seven years of severity dragged them- selves through, the record of which makes a pitiful display upon the pages of English history. There was little inclination on the part of the ejected ministers to escape dis- comfort, their view being, in Richard Baxter's words, that having been ordained to preach they must preach, and. accept the suffering as part of their calling. Like the Apostles they must" obey God rather than men" and afraid to lay down their ministry they preached to such as would hear them in fields and private houses till they were apprehended and cast into jail, where many of them perished." It was his own lot to languish in prison and to write imperishable verses and words of comfort there. John Bunyan spent twelve years in Bedford Gaol and beguiled the days by writ- ing his " Pilgrim's Progress." John Milton, old and blind, beat out the deep music of "Paradise Lost" and "Samson Agonistes " from a bruised and disappointed heart.

div.head: SECOND CONVENTICLE ACT.
div.p: THE SECOND CONVENTICLE ACT.

In 1668 the Conventicle Act expired and Nonconformity, no longer fearful Of the spy and informer began to reveallits full strength. So great was the activity and so numerous the meetings that Sheldon, who 'had become Archbishop of Canterbury, was thoroughly alarmed. Strong pressure was put upon the King and a proclamation appeared under the royal seal enforcing all the previous acts which had been directed against Dissenters. Parliament thanked the King for this and at once passed a second Conventicle Act more effective than the first. It had a clause of unusual candour which set forth as plainly as words could express it that Nonconformity was to be extin- guished by Act of Parliament. "If any doubt should arise concerning the meaning of any part of this Act, it was to be determined in the sense that was the most contrary to Conventicles, it being the inten- tion of the House to repress them in the most effectual manner possible." But the second Conventicle Act was short lived. Charles had followed an unpopular foreign policy and was feeling the embarras- ment of the Dutch war. He was shrewd enough to see that he had been badly advised in the policy of persecution, and to the astonishment of the nation announced in 1672 the Declaration of Indulgence.

div.head: DECLARATION OF INDULGENCE.
div.p: THE DECLARATION OF INDULGENCE.

The motive of the King in making this change of policy may have becn wider than the regaining of popularity. He was a Roman Catholic at heart and his bold step towards the toleration of Dissent may have been part of a plan to secure toleration for Romanism. Whatever the motive his arguments prevailed with his Cabinet and on March 15th, 1671-2, at a time when Parliament was not sitting, the famous document was issued from the Palace of Whitehall. The chief clause in the Declaration said : That there may be no pretence for any of our subjects to continue their illegal meetings and Conventicles, we do Declare, that we shall from time to time allow a sufficient number of places as shall be desired, in all parts of this our Kingdom for the use of such as do not conform to the Church of England, to meet and assemble in, in order to their publick Worship and Des otion ; which places shall be open and free to all Persons. But to prevent such Disorders and Inconveniences as may happen by this our Indulgence, if not duly regulated, and that they may be the bet ter pro- tected by the Civil Magistrate, our express Will and Pleasure is, that none of our Subjects do presume to meet in any Place, until such Place be allow'd ; and the Teacher of that Congtegation be approv'd by us. This meant, in a few words, that buildings might be licensed for dissenting worship, provided that both the minister and the building were approved by the King. The Declaration was made, as we have said, by the King and Cabinet. As soon as Parlia- ',lent met it was repudiated and at once revoked, but it is important to our present study because under its protection Noncon- formity took definite shape. The permission was in force for less than a year, but the congregations that gathered under its sanc- tion were never disbanded. Of its reception by the Nonconformists and its far-reaching results we must now give some account.

div.head: DILEMMAS AND TRILEMMAS.
div.p: DILEMMAS AND TRILEMMAS.

We have no knowledge of the movements of Robert Yates under the Five Mile Act, nor have we in the absence of a diary or letters, his opinion upon the Declaration. That it was received with varying feelings and varying results we gather from those who did place their thoughts upon paper. It will be interesting to quote from two intimate friends of Robert Yates, with both of whom he entered into fullest confidence. We take first the reasoning of Adam Martindale the ejected minister of Rosthern. This year viz. March 15th 1671-2 came out the Kings Declaration of Indulgence to all sorts of Dissenters, allowing to all, save Papists, only their public licensed places, and to them their liberty in private. . . . And I did so little like an universall toleration, that I have oft said, and once wrote in answer to a booke, that if the King offered me my libertie, upon condition that I %you'd consent that Papists, Quakers, and all other wicked sects should have theirs also, I think I should never have agreed to it. (Note. We should not for our own personall libertie, promote a public mischiefe.) But seeing the King's License did not help to clear my way to dos that which I would have done without it, if I could have been suffered. . . and that the Papists and all others must have their liberties whether' I would or nos; I resolved to take mine that I may helpe to counterworke them. (Note. n hereticks be active in overthrowing truth, we should be as vigorous in defending it.) So I had a License for the House of Humphrey Peacock of Morice, when I preached twice every and a lecture once a month; and (so oft Lord's-day, slciy' could conveniently doe it) I ended both my sermons so scone that myself and others might hear my successsors afternoon sermon. The passage incidentally shows that tolera- tion was an unfamiliar and much suspected principle, but the reasoning is shrewd. Different in tone is the account written by Henry Newcombe, formerly of Gawsworth, but then in Manchester. They had the news on March 19th and he writes: Many thoughts of heart there were about it, and various, we being surprised with it. But as soon as I could get; any account from London how matters went, and which way his Majesty would give out licence, I did resolve to endeavour for it, both in conscience of my own duty to preach the Gospel, as also of this people's need of more help than I could afford them in my fullest liberty. On the 19th of April eighteen ministers met in Manchester, Robert Yates being almost certainly among them, to discuss the matter. Their feeling was favourable and they decided in a letter to the King to express their thanks. Newcombe had already sent for a licence for his own house and writes, April 21st. I had an account of a licence granted and therefore I preached in mine own house with doors opened . . . But my licence was only for my own house, which would

attain no end for its incapacity. . . • My licence for the barn came to me May 13, and the Lord's day after (19th) I preached there and so on Wednesday after. After supper Constable Barlow served me with a warrant to appear the next day before the Justices about our preaching. They bad a design against me, supposing that I bad adventured to preach iii the barn on my licence for my house. I had no cause to pre- sume so far. When I appeared and showed my licence they had no more to say to me; and 80 I was delivered of that fear. PHILIP HENRY'S TRILEMMA.

Philip Henry put his CaS-e—ii-e—a:iis;---when he described himself as in a " trilemma," "either to turn Independent in practice, or to strike in with the conformists, or to sit down in silence and suffering." But the longing to preach the Gospel overcame other feelings and he escaped his " trilemma " by taking out a licence.

These reasonings must have passed in varied forms through the minds of the Non- Conformists and large numbers decided as did these worthy and eminent men. Many, in an overflow of generous emotion, sent addresses of gratitude, 'flattering and almost servile in tone. A steady stream of applica- tion poured into the palace of Whitehall to be as quickly granted. From the largo number preserved among the State Papers we select one which is typical of all and of great local interest. The date is April 27th 1672.

John Gleave John Norman Richard Birchall Thomas Widdows James Bate John Bate Th. Ellam THE LICENCES.

The places for which licences were asked were varied and many. Private houses were chosen, so also were barns and malt houses. Meeting houses, specially built, began to spring up, one of them at Sankey, which received its sanction on September sth. The licences given under the Indulgence were of three kinds. The first was for a building duly described. For the congrega- tion meeting there a " Teacher ' was licenced. A third kind was for a "Teacher in general and at large," which allowed the holder to preach in any licensed building, no matter where situated.

Little difficulty seems to have been experi- enced in getting the certificates. A small lee of five pence was charged and as a letter of the period significantly says: "the Dorekeepers and under Clarkes " were "remembered by a token of love."

div.head: AN INTERESTING VOLUME.
div.p: AN INTERESTING VOLUME.

The official register in which the granting of licenses was entered now rests in the Record Office. It is an interesting and well preserved manuscript and teemsiwith famous names. No one could have desired better companionship than Robert Yates enjoyed when asking the favour of license. Two names alone make the great company ever- lastingly famous. It is recorded: Licence to John Banyon to be a Congr Teacher in the howse of Josias Roughead, 9 May Bedford. _
Richard Baxter a Nocconforming Minister to teach in any licensed or allowed place, Oct. 27,11372.

The entries show that the earliest licences were granted on April 2nd, 1672 to London preachers. They close on the 3rd day of the following February. Nearly three hundred crowded pages are filled by the entries and the items number about 3500. Lancashire asked for licences for 86 build- ings of which 17 were meeting houses specially built or adapted. Lancashire preachers numbered 52. Cheshire licences were issued to the total of 83, a large number when the sparseness of the population is remembered. With so great eagerness did dissenters take the opportunity of Royal shelter.

Robert Yates, which suggests that these three firm friends may have acted in unison. That they were five months behind some of their more eager fellows may have been due to an unwillingness to receive any such thing as a permission to preach from the hands of the King. Many preachers refused to allow that the King could either confer or take away a duty- that was imposed by the King of Kings. This argument was presented very strongly by Richard Baxter and explains his own late application. Few of the Baptists and none of the Quakers would recognize the Indulgence at all. It will be noted that Robert Yates is licensed as a "General" preacher, and that he first licensed his own house. Possibly its limited accommodation led to the application for the licensing of the Court House a few weeks later.

The dwelling which thus became the home of the first Nonconformist congregation can- not be identified but the Court House was a central and prominent building of old Warrington and merits fullest description.

div.head: THE_ OLD COURT HOUSE.
div.p: THE_ OLD COURT HOUSE.

The Court House stood on part of the site of thepresent Market Hall, and at the spot long occupied by the Fire Bell. The south wall was part of Cheapside and it faced upon a small square known as the Little Corn Market.

It was a venerable-looking building of red sand-stone. The fine old stones would, in- deed, have proclaimed it a very ancient building, but the antiquarian who had under- taken` to decide its age thereby would have fallen into error. It certainly was an old structure and had served at least two centuries of usefulness. But its stones were much older, for they had been carried from the Old Friary of St. Austin in Bridge-street. At a period when the Friary had fallen into ruin some of its pillars and stones had been thus re-used. Two pillars were re- erected, and supported a lofty tower of ecclesiastical design. Those who may care to consult Dumbevand's painting of old Warrington which hangs in the Antiquities room of the Museum may identify the I square tower that lifts itself prominent above the house tops. An outside flight of stone steps gave access to the court room. Here Sir Thomas Boteler the founder of the Free Grammar School and his successors, the Lords of Warrington, held their manor courts over which their representative, aided by a jury, presided to try cases of debt, to settle disputes between the tenants and to deal with those charged with assault or trespass. Here also the lord of the manor met his tenants on out- standing occasions.

The building would be the central one in the old town. It was the Court of justice and as such would witness many dramas; its bell gave the alarm of fire and for cen- turies sounded the curfew at night.

THE CURFEW BELL. Though the Court House has completely vanished a connecting link remains, very familiar to Warrington ears. When the old building was removed and the Court began to sit at the Bridewell in Buttermarket-street the bell was removed to the Trinity Church Tower and it still rings the Curfew and pro- claims the hours. The tones which float over Warrington at eight each evening are from the same bell that rang over the heads of the worshippers who gathered to listen to the sermons of Robert Yates. No inanimate object ever belonged to the life of a community more completely than this old bell belongs to the life of Warrington. It is just two and three-quarter centuries old, and during its long day has tolled for the famous dead, chimed the curfew, sounded the alarm of fire, called to worship and marked
FROM COTTAGE TO CABINET.
THE EARLY HOME OF THE RIGHT HON. D. LLOYD GEORGE.

Criccieth, in Carnarvon, is a pleasant little holiday resort, with some magnificent views, and is close to some of the best known places in Wales. It has become widely known, however, for another reason. It was in this neighbourhood that Mr. Lloyd George spent his boyhood. Here is the little chapel which he attended thrice every Sunday as a lad, and in which, at the age of sixteen, he was baptised. A mile and a half away is Llany- stumdwy, a picturesque little village, to which thousands of holiday makers pay a visit in order to see the cottage to which Mr. Lloyd George was brought, at two years of of age, by his widowed mother when his first home in Pembrokeshire was sold up. Truly pathetic stories attach to the removal and settlement of the family with the good- hearted bachelor uncle at Llanystumdwy. "My mother," says Mr. Lloyd George, " had to make a hard struggle to bring up her children, but she never complained and never spoke of her struggles. It was not until long after that we were able to appreciate how fine had been her spirit in her task af bringing up her fatherless children."

It is not to be wondered at that Mr. Lloyd George has spoken so sympathetically of those who find it hard to make both ends meet. "Our bread," he said, speaking of those early days, "was home made. We scarcely ever ate fresh meat. I remember our greatest luxury was half an egg for each child on Sunday mornings," Those who have been to Llanystumdwy and have seen the humble little dwelling, have found residents who speak of Mr Lloyd George with the deepest affection and still talk of his adventurous boyhood. Here he lived the ordinary life of a cottager's boy, speaking the pure idiomatic language of the Welsh peasantry, and spending his leisure in woods and the hills. Many stories are told of his daring exploits, and it is said that scars which he still bears are witness to their authenticity._

A short distance from the cottage is the National school. Twice every year the children were marched to the Parish Church to recite the Creed and to be examined in the Catechism. It is recorded that young Lloyd George overhearing his uncle declaiming against this practice, planned a mutiny, with the result that when the boys got to Church they refused to repeat the Creed and were never marched there again for that purpose. Thus in his earlier years he showed that bold combative spirit which has made him so formidable an antagonist in educational conflicts.

• How the little Welsh lad grow to manhood and won his wa3 to the front in politics is a long and fascinating story, but this humble Welsh home had surely not a little to do with the shaping of his career.

Twelve little ;owls fly by in a row— Silent and dark their flight ; Gray little things with shadowy wings, And these are the hours of the night. REDUCED INSURANCE. -A SPECIAL ORDER FOR EMPLOYEES OF LOCAL AUTHORITIES.

The National Health Insurance Commissioners have issued a draft special order enabling local authorities and certain other public bodies to adopt the provisions of section 47 of the National Insurance Act in respect of employees who are entitled to not less than a week's notice. An authority wishing to pay the reduced contribution allowed under the section Must undertake t) pay to all employees covered by the notice full remuneration during sickness for a period not exceeding six weeks in the twelve months, in the manner laid down in the Act. In return for the authority undertaking this liability the ordinary rates of contribution will be reduced by 2d. a week in the case of men (to 5d.) and by I a week (to 40) in the case of women. The employer's share of the contribu- tion will be reduced by id. for a man end id. for a woman, and the employee's shate, whether man or woman, will be reduced by Id.
FIRE AT A LIVERPOOL STATION. BOOKING HALL IN DARKNESS.

A fire broke out on Wednesday rapt at the Central Station, Liverpool, but fortunately it was not serious. A blaze from the roof on the front of the building, directly over the general offices, attracted attention. When the Fire Brigade arrived they were not long in extinguishing the fire. The booking hall was in dark- ness and the station gates were closed. Most damage was done by water. The origin of the fire is unknown.

div.head: LATE MR. T. LONGDIN.
div.p: THE LATE MR. T. LONGDIN.
FUNERAL AT HILL CLIFFE.

In the peaceful and prettily situated burial ground at Hill Cliffs the funeral took place on Saturday afternoon of the late Mr. Thomas Longdin, Borough Surveyor, whose tragically sudden death at the Town Hall the previous Wednesday created widespread regret. The respect in which the deceased gentleman was held by all associated with public work in War- rington was evidenced by the large and repre- sentative attendance at the obsequies. The Mayor and members of the Corporation met at the Town Flail and joining the cortege in Sankey-street, walked to Holy Trinity Church, where the first part of the funeral service was held. Heading the pro- cession were a detachment of police, in charge of the Chief Constable (Mr. M. Nicholls) and Chief Inspector Williameon, and the Fire Brigade under the direction of Superintendent Turner, Aseistant Superintendent F Turner. The employees in the Borough Surveyor's depat tment mustered in full force t.) pay a last tribute to their late chief whose kindliness and geniality made him popular with them all. The service was of the simplest possible character, there being no music. The officiating clergy were the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and the Rev. Lynn Parry. Many members of the Council and officials nroceedel to Hill Cliffs to witness the last rites but those who found it impossible to attend the interment accompanied the cortege as far as Chester-road.

The principal mourners were : —Mr H W Longdin, son (Anerley SE.), Mr Thomas Longdin, son (Ruabon), Mr E S Garland, son-in-law ; Mr B Lowe, Mr A Lang, (Gourock) Mr Joseph Owen (Ruabon), and Mr J Longland. Others who walked in the procession were : Mr Mansfield Cobb, resident engineer for the Warrington Bridge and representing Mr J J Weaver; Mr Philip Thorne, representing Messrs Alfred Thorne7and Sons, contractors for Warrington Bridge works; Mr C A Hindle, quantity surveyor for the Baths extension and and other municipal undertakings; Mr F T Bennie (of Messrs Bennie and Thompson), Mr M S Gaiter, sanitary inspector at Fleetwood; Mr W Walker, architect; and Mr J Swinton, surveyor to the Runcorn Rural District Council.

Vi fol. MICIIITA ILEMBItYBDI
BY MRS. COMYNS CARR
Author of Paul Crew's Story," "Margaret Maliphant," "A Mcdel Wife," "Cottage Folk," "John Fletcher's Madonna," &e.

He was a handsome bird; no one could deny that. He had a brilliant green body, shot with yellow in the breast, gaudy golden touches under the wings, and a peacock-blue head. But his viciousness was beyond compare, and hie language—well, it was choice but not delicate! Nevertheless, Miss Hester was very proud of him. He had been given to her by a soldier fresh from the Front, who had come out of hospital to lodge awhile in the farm- house upon the hill. How the soldier had bought him of some- body, in exchange for somethineelse, to wile away the long horrors of " bUipboard," was a rambling and curious tale. Anyhow. there he was, and the soldier, fascinated by Mies Hester's soft grey eyes and contradictory but bewitchingly mocking laugh. had given him to her as the only gift that he had to give. And Miss Heater adored him. Some folk cruelly said it was because the soldier had got well and had gone away and "had never spoke no word." But folk will be ill-natured, and that is as may be. Anyhow, the parrot was pampered, and no mistake! He spent his time in a smart cage— which it had taken all Miss Hester's savings to purchase—swinging under the cottage eaves, or sunning himself in the hot August afternoons on the top of the lien-coop; and his language, and his vulgar imitations of smack- ing kisses and the drawing of corks, were a scandal—or a delight, according to taste— to all the villagers that came by. "'Tis a good job," said Mrs. Wain at the Bank Farm, "as Grant's holding do lie so far up away from the road, for that brute o' Hester's is enough to shame a respectable woman's house." • It was a queer thing that a girl so well brought up as Hester, who could write a beautiful hand, and play the piano, and curl her hair o' Sundays, should be f3O fond of such an ill-spoken creature! Tom Bunco thought it particularly queer. To him she had always been the complete personification of culture ever since she had come home from boarding-school three years ago. He had almost thought it unbefitting her dignity to make the butter on her uncle's farm, and always looked to her to use longer words than any other girl in the village. And to see her standing there on the threshold laughing till her pretty, proud face was flushed at hearing " Jim " make fun of .him all the time that he was coming up the steep path from the brook, hurt his feelings less than it shook his faith in her perfect re- finement. But it was a sturdy faith and took a deal of shaking. It had been growing silently and steadily for over a twelvemonth, during the whole of which time he had been slowly making up his mind that Miss Hester would make a suitable and proper wife for a man who, after years of patient toil, was at last going to attain the height of all ambi- tion in a hideous two-etoreved house, fifty- _ . . . •..

, fourth in a row, well within the smoke of the manufacturing town where he had daily gone to labour, and far from the peaceful country home whence he had sped at dawn, and whither he had returned at night, and where now he might have spent his maturer days. All through those many railway trips he had pondered on Miss Hester, and he had made up his mind at last that she was worthy. Was a paltry parrot going to disturb his faith or his plans? Not if Tom Bunee knew it! Yet it was disturbing. It was not that he minded being laughed at. Ile was not afraid of many things—not ha! But his mind just misgave him a tiny bit as to whether a lady—worthy of the post of his wife—would so have laughed. But "it's dogged as does it," said be to himself. And he persevered. Yet it was disturbing. Every time he got near the farm he was conscious that, instead of thinking what he would say to Miss Hester. he was puzzling his head as to how he should avoid her parrot. He would approach the farm leisurely, and, with a careless air, from the road; he would climb the field hastily and scale the wall into the farmyard behind; he would stroll up by the brook and steal warily through the orchard. But, wherever he effected an en- trance, the parrot would always be the first to see him, and to fetch the delighted divinity to the window with his horrid welcome: "Oh, you ugly beast!" It was a disheartening ayinouncement. It was enough to put any man out of counten- ance.

For the worst of it was that Tom Bunco was half afraid it was true ! He had never thought much aboui; his per- sonal appearance. Other things being equal, a woman was as well comely; but what did it signify whether a man was so? He had always held that women looked to the mind In you, that it was more manly to be hard. favoured, and that, moreover, a safe bank- ing account, however humble, was better than a straight set of features. But since the parrot's persistent criticism on his outward man he had taken to observ- ing himself in the mirror, and he was troubled with a misgiving lest a bald head, a large nose, protruding teeth, and a freckled countenance might not be atoned for by the showy suit and tasty tie that should whisper of the aforesaid pleasant credit-sheet.

He considered the advisability of having the protruding front teeth replaced by one of the guinea sets" sold by the dentist behind the factory, and thought of paying his ad- dresses in his hat. He wiehed the parrot would vary his form of abuse. And every morning, as he sat in the train, and every evening as he trudged from the station, he turned over in his mind the various methods of avoiding the bird and approaching his mistress undisturbed. At last he hit upon a plan. He would visit Highlow at night! At night even a parrot must sleep. There was a moon—one might approach for greater safety by the back way—and it had always been held to be a romantic thing to make love by the light o' the moon. With a quite new courage he donned his best and set forth. The night, however, was misty. All along the river, and far up the course of the brook that babbled down the side valley, sheets of vapour lay soft and white, and the shapes of trees black, yet uncertain, upon them. It was easy to miss; one's way—even a way that one knew so well. But Tom Bunco was not to be deterred. Sunshine had served him but ill; a dim light might suit him better. He breasted the dark wood bravely; but when he found himself at the top at last, it was only to see that a high wall divided him from hie lady's bower. He paused—sorely tempted to indulge in One of those vulgar forms of expression for which he was wont to condemn that vile bird. But he was not the man to be daunted by a mere wall, when he knew that on the other side of it stood the kitchen-door, behind which his divinity was probably sitting at her needle after the servant had gone—by good chance, alone, and, at all events, out of ear- shot of that cruellest of ecofTers whose cage hung in the front parlour. Tom was inclined to stoutness. Moreover, his thriftiness disinclined him to risk his new

emtnes against the mossy surface of the wall. But there were two or three protruding stones which would help him in the ascent, and he determined to risk it. He put a foot on the first stone' on the second, and, from the third, pulled himself up by his hands and got one leg over the top. But lo! what what his dismay when he saw, on looking down, that the ground, which was sloped up to the wall on the wrong aide, was far below him on the right, and that the sur- face, moreover, was quite smooth here, so that he could only get down by some sliding inoyemenc- wnion would be detrimental to both garments and person. Cautiously he drew the other leg over the top and ruefully considered his next movement.

Nut es 114 at perched thcri, persptring, uncertain, aud inwardly cursing, Miss Hes- Gar's voice broke suddenly out of the dark- ness, chilling him with mortification and de- spair. That she should lee him in such a plight! And yet, of course, she must have seen him, dark as it was, for to whom else could she be speaking? "Go away!" she was saying, and tears and anger struggled in her muffled tones. "Whoever gave you leave to come at such a time of night, and when you knew uncle was away at the fair? I tell you I don't want you. It's like y-,tur impudence to suppcse I would! What have I ever done to be so—so mortified? But it's all the fault of that horrid parrot. Oh! how I wish I'd never ac- cepted him!" Toe blood ran cold in .his veins.
She" had discovered him before he was P2ady. Yee, spite of the darkness she must have done so.

Well, here was a dismissal indeed! And a more bitterly humiliating one than he could have dreamt of! But oh! how right she was to say it was all the fault of that horrid bird! He was a fool to suppose that, if she had flouted him in broad daylight, she would be kinder io him for trying to trap her. Yet "tmpudenre"? That was a bit too strong to a man with honourable intentions Las as she must know them well enough to be. She mortified, indeed!

He tried to look dignified, to balance him- self easily so as to be able to eit as upright in body as he felt in spirit. But the wayward moon, which till now had sheltered behind a cloud, rode mockingly forth, shining full upon him; and, alas! he felt he was not equal to the searching ordeal. When, lo! just as he had cleared his throat to reply, that cruel bird, whom as least he thought he had evaded, burst into a chuckle of scoffing laughter. Oh, untoward Fate! As if the situation were not unlucky enough without that ! And it seemed to him to-night ns though the laughter had in it something uncanny, something strangely human; it was even dis- quieting, paralyeing. It utterly finished poor Tom Bunee. He raised his hand to loosen his collar, and the action was his final undoing. He lost his balance, and fell with a heavy thud right into the middle of a clump cf nettles that clung to the walla beyond Miss Hester's cabbages. The laughter stopped, and there VMS a little cry.

"Mercy me!" cried Miss Hester. Even in the stress of the situation Tom Bunco wondered that the expression was taught in a proper boarding-school; but he NV 2.8 too buoy trying to pick himself out of the mud and the nettles with a sprained ankle to think deeply, and it was a miserable face that he lifted to his lady, who was now stand- ing—with open mouth and wondering eyes— full in the moonlight upon the doorstep. There was a pause. Not even the parrot spoke. Then "Bunce!" said she; and he was too wretched to remark how full of amaze- ment was her tone. "I —I was just taking a little evening walk up the hill, Miss Hester," tattered the un- lucky man, "and—and I thought I'd take a short cut and look in on you. I'll allow it's not the right way to come, and a bit late, too. But, honour bright, I didn't know your uncle was out, miss. I'll—l'll—l'll call some other time. You'll excuse me for saying I never meant to be impudent. I couldn't be such a thing to yea,, miss." In his most real and earnest desire to con- vince her of his true love and unwavering re• spect, he quite forgot how absurdly anything like sentiment must sit upon his disfigured face and dilapidated 'appearance. A little smile curled her pretty lips, and he. never guessed that it was not altogether a mocking one; never guessed that, ridiculous as his appearance was, it was more welcome to her at this particular moment than it ever had been, or than he would ever guess it was! No! Tom Bunce certainly did not im- agine how wonderfully propitious was the moment of an entry which he deemed so disastrous. _

" Well, upon my word. I should have thought the front door would have suited you better," said she, unable to keep from her usual "chaff." " But I won't say as it's ex- actly impudence that I'd accuse you of for not choesing it!"
She laughed merrily; the notion of an pudent Tom Bunee seemed altogether too much for her.

"You lways did find something in me to laugh at, miss," said the poor men, trying in rain to get to his feet. But I'm sure I wouldn't mind if it amuses you. so long as you'd take me serious in one thing." Her laughter stopped short, and he fancied her face softened„ _ _ . _

But, lo! just like his luck—that wretched bird broke in again and spoilt his chance. "You ugly fool !" it Bald this time, and again in euch a horribly human voice that it froze hie meagre courage. lie had prayed for a variant on its usual form of abuse, but this was scarcely an improvement! _ . . .

An expostulation rose to his lips. Oh! that for once she would turn and bid the madden- ing creature be silent. And what wltAs his astonishment when, be- fore lie could speak again, she did it! "Hold your tongue !" she cried, and her voioe positively trembled V% ith anger. "I tell you I'm tired of you. I don't want ever to see or hear you again. Can't you understand plain English? " Tom's mouth grew wide with amazement— but he was half-inclined to laugh too; it seemed so odd to suppose that a bird could understand English like a human being.
Nevertheless, the creature actually seemed to do &P.

He had always hatc,d it for being to clever befo-re, but now he was thankful for its gifts. She had turned her back on Tom Biome and stood on her threshold, her head high, one white arm bared to the elbow, pointing majestically within. She had never seemed to him so lovely. "Out you go! That way!" she said. "And take the wretched thing with you." She vanished into the cottage. "Hang the ugly beast !" muttered a surly voice.

• Wag it the parrot's? And he fancied he heard footsteps within. lie made an heroic effort to get to his feet, but fell back with a loud groan. It brought her to his side. There was the slam of a door shutting on the road yonder, and directly afternards she ran out of the house towards the spot where he sat, crippled. " Why, Mr. Mince, I declare you're hurt," cried she. "And me foolin' with that—that creature! Whatever shall I do? "

He forgot to notice that excitement sent her to the vernacular, he was so pleased at the excitement. "I don't mind, miss," declared he, etontly lertetwaye, not except as it disable me from assistin' of you. But would you ex. euse me Wan' what you might ha' done with that thers bird? "

Her pretty head drroned so that he could not see her face. " He's gone," answered she, in a low voice. " Hell never molest . . folk again. He wrs ill-brought up. He could know better, p'raps. I can't think how he ever amused me. But I'm sick to death of him now."
" Vraps he was ill-brought up," mused Tom, but he was clever! My! He did understand English, Fhe as it might ha' bin you or me. But it was plain English, and no mistake!"
He looked at her, but her head drooped lower still, and, in spite of the hopeful glow at his heart, he did not feel that he had won quite far enough yet to dare to raise it.

- "Any way, he did understand," said she. "And he's gone, and he'll never come back any more, so let's say no more about it, but just forget him. Come, let me help you in- doors, Mr. Mince. There's uncle comb' in. He'll be sore put about to ace you in trouble. Uncle has a great respect for you, Mr. Bunco." She got him to his feet, and he limped to- wards her home, leaning on her firm. young shoulder. " You'd little think what I come 'ere to say to-night, miss," whispered he, emboldened by her kindness and her near nroximitv;. " And its little nt I molt to say it, surely." Two days ago she would have laughed loudly, and that horrid parrot would have c;.:lnied her. But to-night she only said: "Handsome is as handsome does, Mr. Bunco." Upon which Tom Bunce found a good deal more to say than he had ever said before, and said it in plain English too. By which it may be surmised that whatever he had for a moment suspected, he was so well con- vinced that MISS Hester's plain English had been well understood that he never did "say any more about it," and forgot the very existence of that obnoxious bird in the kind smiles of its mistress. For whether it was tile banking account anu "uncle's great respect," whether it was the foot and new suit of clothes damaged in the bold quest of her, or whether it was the rousing of a sudden tender pity at a cowardly and unfair onslaught, none .ever knew; but sure it was that something in the uncouth figure claimed her wayward woman's qmpathy, and won her heart in the process, and that Tom Bunco rode in an easy winner at the last, to the amazement of all who knew Miss Hester's sprightly spirit. True, her saucy tongue was never tired of Its merry raillery; but the raillery—being tier very own—was never anything but a iouroe of pride to her lover. And when she settled down to the head of that table of which he thought so much, her husband was often heard to say that it was only your true lady who dared venture on repartee;. but that if man or beast ever went too far his wife knew how to make them understand plain English, in a way which, Tom BLUM darkly hinted, it was a lesson to hear.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Harvest Festivals.—Varions opinions have been expressed as to the appropriateness of holding harvest festivals in a year of damaged crops, and the question of praying for floe weather. In early Victorian times such a failure of the harvest as mlny districts have witnessed this summer would have been most serious for the general public, and would have moved people to appeal for Divine help. But there is not now the same dependence on the home harvest, and there is less dis- position in those times to resort to prayers relating to natural processes. Then, although the harvest has been disappointing, and indeed ruinous to a largo number of agriculturists, many of the harvests in the Colonies and other countries winch supply us with food-stuffs, have been exceptionally good, and the general opinion appears to be that the thanksgiving festivals in the churches should be held as usual. For the bountiful harvests in other lands we have more reason to be thankful than if the season at home had been a good one, and to suspend the thanksgiving services because of our own misfortunes, would be indeed to weigh out our piety in golden scales:

WOmen- arid Municipal Affairs.—The laws of our country hays declarod th t a woman is not "a person" and despite The Qualification of Women Act of 1907, there is still much ambiguity concerning the status of the married woman* Some of the revising barristers still hold that marriage disqualifies a woman from serving on a town or borough council. This is not the general interpretation of the law, but it sometimes has the effect of depriving a married woman of her vote, 'and of her right to stand as a candidate. This is an lanomaly which should be put right, as it is not fewer, but more women who are wanted to take an active interest in municipal alttirs. Mrs Humphrey Ward recently called attention to this subject. There are only twenty-one women on all the county and borough councils of the UniteJ Kingdom, and on more than two hundred Boards of Guardians there is not a single woman member. It is to bo hoped that the forthcoming elections will show a better state of things. There is in this country a very large number of women in easy circumstances, mho have the necessary time, education, sod intelligence, to render useful public service in the management of local government affairs. Sweated Labour.—Not long ago, it was :announced that conceited measures were to be taken by the Government to raise the low standard of wages, in the " sweated trades." The chief sufferers in these ill- paid industries are the women and girls—homeworkers employed in the making of " ready-to-wear" clothing, ties, aprons, etc.—and according to Miss Young, a lady sanitary inspector for one of the Loudon boroughs, the Trade Boards Act, has made no appreciable difference to their earnings. As examples of some of the pre- vailing rates, in the best London trade, she says that for making elaborately-trimmed blouses, or camisoles, composed of fine insertion and lace trimming, home- workers are paid Is. 6-1. a dozen. For heavy cloth mantle., well-finished, with buttons, and button-holes, 7d. each, and for bathing costumes with braided jackets and knickers, lid. each. It is little wonder that with such starvation rates, the " homes 'where the work is carried on are very often far from what they ought to be, and that this state of things involves some danger to the public health. Fear of loss of work prompts a denial of cases of consumption, or infectious disease, with the result that the goods when sent out, may become fruitful sources of dissemination. It was thought:that the Trade Boards Act would do something V) mitigate the evils resulting from " sweated labour ' but apparently, that is not the case so far as outsvorkers are concerned.

Fashions and Commerce.—Lyons, the great silk manu- facturing centre in France, echoes the bitter cry of many other manufacturing towns against the hobble skirt mode. According to the report, of its Chamber of Commerce,this was responsible for a greatly reduced silk manufacture last year, which amounted to only £15,500,000, compared with £18,000,000 in 1910. Lyons is therefore, like many of our own textile manufactur- ing towns yearning for the departure of the prevailing fashion which dispenses with silk linings, and under- skirts. Fashions have a way of going from one extreme to the other, manufacturers have been buoyed up with repeated promises of changes which however lag by the way, and the " woman in the street" stilt clings to a walking costume which demands only half of the material that went to its making three or four years ago. Milliners have no grievance on the same Score,— but they too are complaining that lady motorists wear "almost anything"—not only when driving but at other times and that the custom—being followed by others— Is not good for the millinery business. New Sleeves-- Women who are blessed with rounded arms and shapely hands, can wear short sleeves with complacency, knowing that they lsok well when thus arrayed, and will probably continue to wear what is so eminently becoming to them. But others, to whom nature has proved less kind, will welcome the advent of the long sleeve, which is sten on all this season's newest models, and which is not without its advan- tages, for it is convenient, warm, and comfortable, further more it is distinctly graceful. Any way it is to be the favourite shape this winter, and will come well down over the wrist. Often a deep cuff of a contrasting material, such as velvet, or satin, which is repeated on Co the band and collar, finishes it at the wrist. JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
A GENTLE HINT.

I knew three reporters who, representing different local p were, were often thrown together. Two of them might fairly be described as just average mortals; the third, a comparatively new comer at the time of which I write, was a bit of a bore—for a while. He had an enormous appetite, and was over fond of telling tall stories about his meals. The others, his unwilling not to say resentful auditors, were all the.while on the look-out for a chance to cure him of his bad habit without blurting out exactly what they thought of htm One day the offender came with a wonderful story respecting a tremendous steak pudding which he had just consumed. " Hum," quietly interposed one of his long-sufferers, "that's very r ealarkable. It happens that we have had steak pudding, too. Let me tell ran about it. It was such a monstre pudding—for it is a dish we are all fond of —that my wife decided to boil it in the copper, but the thing was so large that she could not get it in. Luckily, however, the paviors were at work right in front of the hone, so the missis got them to put it on their fire, and "—" Liar ! " growled his victim ; but it did the trick.

THE "BARTHOLOMEW WORTHIE3." The 1662 Ejectment was the subject of pulpit treatment at several local Nonconformiet places of worship on Sunday last. Of the 2,000 conscientious clergy, who in the time of Charles ll° were turned adrift under circumstances elsewhere explained to readers of this paper', a couple of hundred belonged to Yorkshire. Prominent amongst these was Oliver Heywood, who, from the village of Northowram, near Halifax, went forth on missionary journeys in defiance of the cruel acts of intolerant ecclesiastica vigoroutly administered by a bigoted magistracy. One of the districts in which he repeat-dly preached was Stansfield township, on the East Lancashire border line, and as the result of his eflsrts thereabouts a cause was started which eventuated in the erection of a chapel on the hillside. When it became advisable to follow the population into the valley below the old building was converted into four cottages, and these are recopied to-day—or were three weeks ago, when, taking a IrAiday in those pasts, I i attended a commemotative service n the (pen air dose by the vene,able pile. That particular ctlebration of the 250th anniversary, of the great Ej-ctrnent took place quite appropriately on the Sunday following Barthelomewls Day - the very day after, in fact. I could hardly help feeling. therefore, that the War- rington commemoration of the historic eve .t which si,a) I e said to have given rise to organised Noncen- to nay was a Nee belated; but no doubt there were seasons for that— an, how, better late than lot at all. I sometimes wt rider what tho,e3 sturdy forefathers f ours would have tht ught of the health fads that °wet-lays about especially if tie germ theory spec ling di-ease w Ine h we all &ire! y receive vi how cp esti n. At the last eittinge of the General v...sembly of the Welsh Calvinistic Methodisti held at Newt ,ite, Men tgonteryslire, Mr. David Daeiee, originator of the Wtl h anti-consumption campaign, said that apart from monetary assistance the movement cou'd be support. d by those responsible for the erection of chapels seeing that the orottiary laws of sanitation were observed. There were come chapels the is indoets of which could not be cpened. and in crowded chapels much dist ase was spread. The A‘sembly de cid, dto upport the movement sod estaldis• ed a " national Sunday" connected with it. What wou'd our Non- ccnformist ancestors have slid to all this? Then thine are the individual conirnuoion cups which are gradually taking the place or the old servics of p'ate i formerly n universal use. Some of our older folk have little patience with these ianovations. For my- 'self, I think that the changes are decidedly for the better. A few years ago, one of the oldest Magistrates Clerks in the country remonstrated with me for writing in support of the movement for the mo.-ification of the then common form of oath in Court, which involved the kissing of an indiscribtbly filthy Testament which had been weed for the purpose longer than I could remember. Said he "It's all stuff and nonsense. I've never known a single case of consumption to arise from the practice. Obviously, the answer, final and complete, was ready to my haud. RAILWAY SIGNALLING.

The " Examiner" report of the accident at Lynam Station reminded me of the recent completim of an elaborate system of electrical signalling at Snoa -hill Station, Birmingham, whore it forms patt of the extensive reconstruction undertaken by the Great Western Railway Company. The miniature levers of the electrical system, each about Gin, in length, are sot in a frame of such dimensions that two men can have under direct observation the 225 levers that occupy the south box at Snow-hill, whilst one man can direct the 80 at the other end. When the signalmai switches over the points and clears the line for an oncoming train a contact is established which flashes back to his calin an intimation that bin intention has been fulfilled. Then be releases the signal, and in the same way When it falls a circuit is completed which returns him the confirmatory message. Failing this antoniafc reply, it is obvious the signal is set against the trais, and no disaster can result before an investigation of theinterruption has been made. Again, supposing a train has been directed into a certain section on the old system, it was not only possible but happened with disastrous frequency that a signalman in his forgetfulness or worry, unwittingly sent another train into the same section. This is impossible with the electrical installation, because the section is automatically locked after the admission of the first train and a second cannot be turned in. I am in pos,ession of interesting details concerning various types of railway signals, and, as many passengers have no idea of the meanieg of quite a number of these, I may take adrantage of some future opportunity to reproduce the informatiom. A NUISANCE AND ANNOYANCE.

In his magazine reference to talking in church, the Rev. IL B. Firth incidentally remarks that in the concert room people may without objection chat to each other before the performance begins. Oh, of course. It is the chattering too often indulged in by thoughtless patrons during the concert that adds to the haragsed musicians' grievances and so exasperates people who have really gone to enjoy the music and not to listen to cookery recipes or the latest bit of scandal. An old col!eague or mine tells how he attended an oratorio years ago, and unfortunately found himself seated near two over-dressed ladies who were plainly bored by a performance the excellences of which they were quite unable to appreciate, and throughout the earlier part of the pro- gramme talked at such a rate that the critic was distracted. To his great relief, when this bad been going on for an hour or so, the interruptors were " shut up" for the remainder of the evening owing to a singular coincidence. The orchestra were vigorously leading up to a grand climax, and, on account of the blare of the brass and crash of instruments of percus- sion, the animated pair in front, who continued their conversation regardless alike of the progress of the piece and the ccmfort and convenience of their neigh- bours,:raised their voices. Then there occurred a sudden pause in the music, and in loud tones one of the offending ladies was saying to the other : " We fry ours in fat !" This was distinctly audible many rows of scats away, and the unlucky speaker found indignant eyes glaring at her horn all sides. The silly couple were effectually silenced for that evening at least. THE GRAND DUCHESS 010 HESSE. The Grand Duchess of Hesse has hit upon a novel scheme for propagating the know- ledge of how to fight consumption. The Grand Duchess has succeeded in inducing all the match manufacturers in the Grand Duchy to place hints on how to avoid the spread of tubercular contagion, on the back of every match-box they sell.

LORD MAYOR DESIGNATE 08' LIVERPOOL. Mr. John Sutherlard Harrnood Banner, M.P., DL, J.P., who is to be invited to accept the Lord Mayoralty of Liverpool, is a native of Liverpool. He was educated at Hadley College, near Oxford. In 1805 he was appren- ticed to his father, and in 1872 he became a partner of the firm of Harmood Banner and Son, accountants, North John-street, Liverpool, of which he is now head. He is also chairman of Pearson and Knowles, Ltd., colliery proprietors. In 1895 he entered the City Council as a member for Exchange Ward, and his expert knowledge of accountancy, coupled with an extensive experience in the realm of finance, especially fitted him for membership of the Corporation Finance Committee, the chairmanship of which he has held for many years. His comprehensive knowledge of general municipJ administration has been recognised by his election as chairman of the Municipal Corporations Association. His residence is Aston Hall, Preston Brook, Cheshire, and he has filled the office of High Sheriff of the county. He was in 1905 elected M.P. for the Everton Division of Liverpool on the resignation of the late Sir John Willox. new Lady Mayoress is Mr. Harrnood Banner's second wife. She is a charming Irish lady, and her marriage to the member for Everton took place in March, 1908.
