LODGER CLAIM REFUSED. At the evening sitting on Monday. the Barrister refused several claims for lodger votes on the ground of insufficient value. Mr. Harry Rogers,of the Feathers Hotel, claimed a lodger vote in respect of the exclusive use of two rooms. He said he was not employed by his mother, the licensee, but sometimks assisted in the management of the hotel. He had a business of his own.

In reply to the Barrister, Mr Woodcock said he had no idea of the value of hotel, apart from the licence. Mrs Rogers, two daughters,anotner son,and the servant were in residence in the house. The Barrister pointed out that taking away the hotel value there were SIX rooms. "I suppose" he added " the hotel value is everything." Mr Woodcock : Yes ;itis a good one. The Barri.ter : What would it let for, assuming it was converted? Mr Woodcock : I don't know at all. Mr Rogers, answering the Barrister, said he had no written agreement for the rooms. There were two sitting-rooms in the house and one was his own, absolutely. The Barrister : I cannot make this into value,allow- ing for the fact that it is a hotel.

The claim w.s disallowed. A DOC TOR'S LODGER VOTE. DISALLOWED THROUGH ABSENCE. The Liberals objected to the lodger vote of Mr Sydney V. Tinsley, Dalby Villas, Latchford Without. Mr Sanders said his information was that for the past two years Mr Tinsley had beau living in Durham. Mr Joseph Smith, assistant overseer for Latchford Without. said he had a declaration that Mr Tinsley bad occupied the rooms for 12 months. Mr Sanders repeated that Mr Tinsley had lived in Durham for practically the whole of the qualifying period. The Barrister (to Mr Smith) : Do you know, of your own knowledge, that he has occupied the rooms during the qualifying period. Mr Smith : No sir. Nct apart from the declaration. The Barrister : In future, without my having to give the instruction again, all the assistant overseers roust make inquiries about these lodgers and get all the information possible, and they will be allowed it in their expenses. Mr Smith : I have been there and made inquiries. They did not question it at all, as to whether he was in occupation. The Barrister: How long had he been there ? That is the point. Mr Smith: There is a declaration before me, signed by two parties. The. Barrister : Never mind the declaration. Really, r Smith, you ought to know better. These declara- tions, as I have said many a time, are about as much use atlest year's almanac. They are filled up, in nine cases out of ten, by the agents, and the claimants are told to sign them. They do so and they know no more

Mr. Woodward said there were one or two of those parishes who should be brought to book for the constant and chronic neglect of payment. The mischief was that this year things generally had been going fairly well in the outstanding districts and if the money had been applied for systematically and with energy and judgment it would have been called in. It was decided that the chrs write to the various negligent townships in terms which he should think fitting. RUNCORN GIRL'S DOWNFALL. ONE WHO "KNEW THE ROPES." On Wednesday at Manchest.r Police Court Mery Ann Gough (17), of Surrey-street,Runcorn vas again charged with the theft of letters containing postal orders value 308. by means of a trick. Detective best, of the Man- chester police. said Gough was arrested at Middlewich. She at once admitted her identity and confessed to having spent the money on cheap jewellery and finery for herself. The postal orders were, subsequently, found to have been cashed in Chester. Charles Po:vital!, cashier for Messrs. Simpson and Davies and Co.,Runcorn, said the postal orders referred to were dispatched by him to one of their boatmen and addressed care of the Bridgewater Canal Co., Hulme Locks, Manchester, it being customary for their boat- men to call at that point for the remittances. A tonnage clerk said prisoner represented that she had been sent by her uncle for his letters. She gave his name glibly and told so straightforward a tale es to who the senders were that his suspicions were allayed. It was customary, be :said, for boatmen to send messengers for letters. The Clerk : She " knew the ropes " well. Henry Smith, the boatman referred to, said prisoner travelled with him for a few years between Manchester, Runcorn and Eastharn, as companion to his little girl and in that way she became accustomed to his move- ments. Prisoner, who tearfully asked for forgiveness, had ' been remanded in custody for a week arid was now again remanded. Yesterday she pleaded guilty, and on promising to go into a girls' home under the care of a missioner, was discharged.

WEDDING OF MR P LEATHER.—A very interesting and pretty ceremony took pl .ce at the Wesleyan Church on Monday last, the occasion being the ruarrisge of Mr Percy N Leather son of Mr and Mrs A Leather, of Booth's Hill,Lymm. and Niles Kleanor Goodier,daughter of Mr and Mrs A Doodier of Bridgewater-street.Lyrnm. The bride who was charmingly attired in a cream coloured costume with hat to match, was given away by her father. The ;Misses Sarah nod Edith Doodler sisters of the bride, attended Its bridesmaids, and Mr Rowland Dixon performed the duties of beat man. The officiating clergymen was the Rev Pawliu. Mr Harry Brown provided the organ music in his capable style. At th‘r close of the ceremony the local Wesleyens pre- sented the bridal pair with a clock as a token of respect for the bride, who has been a teacher in the Wesleyan Sunday School. The bridegroom is a tr acher and assistant organist at the Congregational Church, and that Mr and Mis Percy Leather are popular was shown by the crowded audience at the ceremony and by the large number of presents they have received. The wedding breakfast was held at Bridgewater-street,after which tee happy couple left for Southport where the honeymoon is to be r pent.

CHOIR Tall' TO BLACKPOOL—On Saturday last the members ot the Oughtrington Parish Church choir were the fortunate participants in a trip to Blackpool. The Vicar, the hev. E. P. Wethered and the organist and choirmaster, Mr. 0. G. Smith accompanied the party. Being favoured with fine weather until about 4.30 p.m. the membeis were able to spend an enjoyable time out of doors, the fairground at South Shore with its many attractions coming in for a good share of their attention. Despite the frequent stops on the return journey which caused a late arrival at Warrington the party were very fortunate in securing a connection at the Low Level station, the train there being conven- iently late. Lymm was reached about 10p.m.

div.head: REVISING THE LISTS. FUTILE PROTEST AGAINST LIBERAL NOTICES OF OBJECTION.
div.p: REVISING THE LISTS. FUTILE PROTEST AGAINST LIBERAL NOTICES OF OBJECTION.
THE BARRISTER AND " MANUFACTURED "
RENT BOOKS.

In view of the drastic measure of electoral reform already introduced in the House of Commons, and which involves a revolution in the system of registra- tion, there is every likelihood that revision courts, as we now know them, will soon be institutions of the past. Mr. C. 11. M. Wharton, the revising barrister who has been going through the list of electors for Warrington this week, takes the view that the Bill will not pass in its present form, hut he freely admits that there is room for improvement in the existing methods of granting the franchise. At the Revision Court which opened at the Warrington Town Hall on Monday morning there were 22 1( dger claims and 18 ordinary occupiers' claims, with the same number of occupier objections. Mr. E. A. Sanders represented the Liberals and Mr. Herbert Hayes was for the Con- servatives. Mr. W. H. Woodcock (assistant over- seer) was also in attendance.

div.head: LIBERAL OBJECTIONS.
div.p: LIBERAL OBJECTIONS.

FUTILE PROTEST BY THE CONSERVATIVES. Before any cases were heard, Mr Hayes contested the validity of the notices of objection sent out by Mr Sanders on behalf of the Liberal party. He said that Mr Sanders objected to the tames of various people on the list as residing at I, Greenbank-street, on the occupiers' list of Parliamentary electors, St Austin's Ward, Polling District No 10, Division 1. His con- tention was that 111 r Sanders was not on the list for St Austin's Ward, and, therefore,had no right to object to any person on the list. He was only on the municipal list in iespect of 1, Greenbank street. ~ The Barrister : Is there any authcrity to show me that if a man is an elector it is necessary that be should be an elector for a particular district before he can object? iNlr Hayes ly contention is that the Act says any person on the list can object to the name of any other person on the list. The Barrister (indicating certain documents).—But the list is this.

Mr Hisses : Does Division 3 mean the same list as Division 1? I contend that they are two separate lists. A burgess may object to a burgess on the list, but to object to a Parliamentary voter he should be a Parliamentary voter. The Barrister : You don't suggest that this man is not a Parliamentary voter, do you ? Mr Hayes: I suggest he is not on the list we are revising es a Parliamentary voter. My contention is that he should be on the list we are revising. There is no other list to be considered at the present moment. The Barrister : You mean the list in existence now? Mr Hayes : My contention is that this is the list he should be on—not the old list.
_ Tbe Barrister : This list which lam going to revise is not in operation at all. It is not the list yet; it is not authorized. . .

Mr Hayes: And that is your decision. The Barrister : It is not authorized. The list authorized is the other list. Mr. Hayes : The law does not specify any list, as far as I can see. It says " Any person on the register of voters." _ . . .

The Barrister : That is the register which is at present in existence and which, if there were a General Election to-day, would be used. Mr Hayes : 1 understand that, but the Act reads that " any person on the list." The Barrister : I tay that is the list. As far as I have heard you, I cannot see anything in the point. Mr Hayes next took exception to what he described as the careless way in which certain notices of objec- tion had been sent out. They were calculated to mis- lead the voter. According to his Honour's ruling, Mr Sanders was on the list for Division 1, nut in the notices in question he descrined himself as only a burgess. The Barrister : I don't see anything in that point either. The greater includes the less. If he is on the list, it is quite sufficient. You must accept my ruling as to the meaning of the word " list." It uoes not mean division 1. 2 or Z. Mr. Hayes : Then any person on tha list can object to another person on the list ? The Barrister,: You must not put into my month anything I have not said. That is an old plsn I have heard quite frequently. At present I'do not seo any substance in the objection. ARE RENT BOOKS "COOKED"?

The old question of rent books as evidence cropped up in a claim made through the Liberals for a Parlia- mentary vote in respect of an occupier's qualification. Mr Sanders explained that the claimant's mother had been on the register for the same house, but the tenancy was trauterred to the son. The name was not altered on the register, because probably it had been taken for granted that the tenant was the same as before. The claimant produced three rent books to prove that he had been the tenant during the qualifying period. Having been informed who was the landlord, Mr Hayes said : I don't think it is right that these rent books should be produced. Some more substantial evidence should be given. I have a case in mind where a landlord signed a declaration that a person was a tenant when he knew very well that he was not.

The Barrister : You 'Lust not make those statements unless you have proof. Mr Hayes : I have got it in their own writing. The Barrister : Here is the rent book. You mean these rent books have all been manufactured for the purpose? Mr Ha)es : I say there is a system in Warrington amongst some landlords— The Barrister: Don't trouble me with systems, . . . . .
please, but if there is any allegation that these books have been deliberately "cooked" for the purposes of this revision, I will listen to you, and very seriously.
"A HARD CASE."

MEDICAL RELIEF AND THE FRANCHISE. The question of disfranchisement through receipt of medical relief was raised in a case brought forward by Mr Sanders. He pointed out that the applicant had received medical relief in respect of his child who was ' a patient in the Workhouse hospital, suffering from epileptic the. The Barrister: Do you say he has received the medical relief? Mr. Sanders: No, the child, through him. It is a very bard case indeed. In reply to the Barrister, the applicant stated that he regularly paid the Guardians Is. per week in respect of the child. That was the arrangement between him and the authorities. Mr. Ssoders produced a medical certi Beate from the doctor who, he said, was desirous of doing all he could for the man. . _ .

Further questioned, the claimant said he began to contribute Is per week when his chili had been in the hospital a fortnight. That was nearly twelve months ago. Have they asked you if you will pay more, or are they content with that?—No, they asked me to pay is., and I consented to it: _ . .

That is all that they asked ?—I told them it was as much as I could afford to pay. The Barrister: I don't see any objection to this. It is a case that seems to be covered by authority and left to my discretion. It is also pointed out in more , than one case that where there is any doubt at all it should be exercised in favour of the claimant to the vote. I shall grant this vote unless there is somebody who can point Out any reason why I should cot. Mr Hayes: I don't object. The vote was allowed. LODGER VOTE ALLOWED—NOT A PRECEDENT. The Conservatives claimed a lodger vote for Mr Frank Rutter, 31, LJvely-lane. He stated that he occupied the bearoom and sitting-room and paid 6s per week for them. Mr Hayes : Mr Rutter was on the list last year, but came off through removing from one lodging to another. In reply to Mr Sanders, the claimant said there was another lodger in the house. Mr Sanders : I think it is against the claimant, if there is another 7lodger in the house and the rateable value is only £l9 10s. It is absolutely fatal. Mr Hayes said Mr Rutter occupied the best rooms in the house. Mr Woodcock said Mr Rutter's was a genuine lodger claim. The only question was as to whether the value was sufficient. The house was a larger one than was usual for the rateable value of £l9 103. It was a ques- tion of establishing a precedent. The Barrister : That is the only point. Mr Sanders : The only thing is, the rateable value is just under £2O. It might be favourable to other claim- ants if allowed. Mr Woodcock : The barrister has not said he would allow every Case over £2O. Mr Sanders said he had no 01-jection, but be bad similar cases and should draw the attention of the Court to them. The Barrister : ram influenced more by the fact that this is a genuine lodger case, and there is no other applicant. But you must please understand that this is not a precedent. I grant this this time, but no-one must remind me that I gave Mr Rutter a vote. "ALL NONSENSE." Later the Barrister had something to say about the unnecessary making of declara- tions to correct literal errors in the list. Addressing the party agents he asked : " Why is it necessary to put these people to the expense of making declarations when you can easily have the spelling put right ?" Mr. Sanders : It is unnecessary trouble. I think you have a perfect right to correct any raisdescription and you have done so up to now. The Barrister : If the person is identified and lam assured it is the same person' it is all nonsense giving people the trouble of making declarations. You gentle- men must understand I have been at your game before to-day, and I have sat in associations where Mr A has
a

The Barrister: You are content to be taken off the register ? Mr Thornton: Yes.
Mr Hayes : He argues that he is entitled, but he doesn't care whether he has the vote or not.
The Barrister: Please allow me to deal with it. (To Mr Thornton) : You don't object to be taken oil the register? Mr Thornton: No.

The Barrister : Very well, there's an end of that point. Mr Thornton explained that his brother was the tenant of the Refuge Assurance Offices on a rental from his father, Mr Henry Thornton. His brother's system of business was to work entirely on commission, and he could, is he so desired, remove the offices to any quarter of the town. He employed a staff of clerks whom he engaged and dismissed, and charged their salaries to the company. The clerks were responsible to him and not to the company. The Barrister said the whole point was whether Mr , Thornton was responsible to the staff for their engage- ment, dismissal and everything. Were they simply there for the purpose of helping to earn his commission or did they help to earn somebody else'a commission as well ?

• Mr Thornton: They are there simply for my brother's commission. Mr Sanders contended that Mr IN E Thornton occupied the office as district manager for the Refuge Assurance Company and th,:t he simply supervised the clerks, but had not power to dismiss them without the consent of the company. Mr Sanders also submitted that as a shareholder of the company Mr Thornton was not entitled to a vote in respect of the premises. The Barrister : You are begging the question. He is not claiming the vote, in any sense of the word, because of his connection with the company. He says " I have got an office. You have nothing to do with why I use it." If you can show that it is not his office or that he is obliged to have that place by the order of his employer, that will be a different matter. Mr Sanders : That is my contention. 'Jibe Barrister : You have not proved either of tho.e points. I'm afraid I an not %All you. You have argued this case very well and raised every possible point that could be raised, but I am against you, and I shall not tab o this name from the register. The vote was allowed.

div.head: BARRISTER AND THE FRANCHISE BILL
div.p: THE BARRISTER AND THE FRANCHISE BILL

On the completion of the revision on Wednesday morning, the Barrister said he might meet them again one more year, but only one. In regaid to the Franchise Bill, personally ho had read it, though not very carefully, but sufficiently to enable him to say he could not realise the possibility of its passing. Whether the methods of revision would be altered or not was another matter. He himself was willing to admit there was much room for improvement. He thought that if the duty of preparing a Bill had been left to revising barristers, having had stated to them clearly what was required iu the way of franchise, they would have got a more workable Bill than the one before the House of Commons, he was afraid that the persons who had charge of the details of the Bill could have had little knowledge of the details of registration or could not have realised the enormous amount of work which was apparently to be thrown on the Town Clerks and other officials. Ile thought the best thing the authorities could do would be to try and do it all over again It must not be forgotten that the party agents would have something to say and the num- ber of appeals to the County Court, as far as he could judge, would be something enormous. He was quite sure that, knowing as he did the amount of work in the County Courts, and the fact that they were now considerably overworked, the suggestion would meet with serious opposition from that quarter. It was not his business to say anything about tne Bill, but he hoped he would never live to see the time when the representation of a great borough like Warrington might be decided by the casting vote of a half-lunatic woman or a man who for every other purpose was considered as undesirable a citizen as it was possible for a man to be. They had another year's grace and perhaps then he might have the opportunity of congratulating them on the fact that they would be in a position to go on swimmingly for a few years to come. He thanked the officials for the way they had helped him in the matter. They had not had much law to discuss, but it had been argued well on both sides, and the arguments bad been a great help to him. He. had again to congratulate the parties upon the fact that he had not made any orders as to costs and he still had the record that during five years of revising, he had only made two orders for costs and those were for 2s. 64. each. His object was to make a clean register and to prevent anything in the shape of squaring a register—no arrangements between parties. If a man was entitled to be on the list he ought to be on,and if he was not entitled he ought not to be on. Whether it was considered wise by one party or the other had nothing to do with bim. A clean register was what he always tried to bring about and in regard to Warrington, there was not a cleaner regis- ter in the country. Mr H Hayes (Conservative agent) in proposing a. comprehensive vote of thanks to the revising barrister and the other officials, spoke of the fair way in which his Honour had listened to what they had had to say. The work became easier as each year passed by,through the assistance of Mr Woodcock and his staff and other officials of the Corporation. He quite agreed with his Honour in regard to the new Bill before tbe House of Commons. He did not think there was any fear of its passing, at any rate, and he thought they would have the pleasure of meeting there for a few more years. Mr Sanders (Liberal Agent) in reconding said that was his first attempt at Revision Court work and he, fully admitted he felt rather nervous at first, but he could safely say that the way Mr Wharton had helped him bad given him courage, which had been renewed at every sitting. He could only speak in very high terms of the fair and impartial way in which Mr Wharton bad conducted each case as between voter and objector. If there had been any slight doubt, the applicant had been given the benefit of it. Of course, he could not agree with the slashing attack made on the Franchise Bill. It might be altered, but it would come into force. He would admit that it would have been better to have taken into account the opinions of revising barristers and overseers, because it was their wc.rs and they would have been able to give expert advice. It was a very intricate work Indeed and could only be carried out by efficient workmen. Not only from the Barrister had be received every kindness and help in that particular branch of agent's work but he could endorse the sentiments of Mr Hayes in regard to the great assistance be had received from Mr Woodcock and his assistants and the Town Clerk's officials. The work. had been carried on in a very creditable manner. The vote was then passed and after some formal business, the Court rose.

Owing, it is believed, to a shot having been left among tbe coal, an explosion in a furnace at the Staffordshire Iron Works, at Walsall, on Wednesday blew out the end of the furnace and scattered bricks and boiling water in all directions. Three men were severely burned and scalded.

div.p: THE ARMY MANCEUVRES.

about the values or the facts than the man in the moon. Mr broith : It is a difficult matter for me to find Out, unless I watch the house. I bad not the slightest doubt that he had been in occupation. I did not ask the question. The Barrister : You had not the slightest doubt but you don't know anything about it, do yeu ? If you don't, say so. What does the landlord,Williara Tinsley. say ? Mr Smith : I did not ask him the question whether his son had lived there twelve months. he Barrister : Where is he now ? Mr Smith: I cannot tell you. Mt Hayes : Heis in Durham. Mr Sanders : I can bring evidence that he has been in Durham for two years. He might have been here for three months out of the qualifyiug year. Mr Woodcock said Mr Tinsley was formerly house surgeon at ‘Varrington Infirmary. He left the district a lung time ago to go out of town but there was no doubt that his home was at Dolby Villas. Mr Smith : I asked Mr Tinsley, senior, the question "Is he the tenant of the rooms ? ' and he raid" Yes," and added that he bad rent receipts. I took it tor granted that he was in occupatiou. Mr Hayes : He has an appointment at Durham, hut he has occupied the rooms during the qualifying period on many occasions. A witness called by Mr Sanders swore that he went to Mr Tinsley's house that afternoon and was told by the servant that Mr Tinsley had not lived there tor two , years. He was at Durham, but came over occasionally. Mr Hayes: My contention is that he has been in the ' lodgings many times during the qualifying period. The witness added that the servant told him Mr Tinsley had been there within the last fortnight, but that he only came over occasionally. The Barrister : It would be a very curious thing if he does not visit his father now and toen. Taut is not the point. Ws want to know whether he is a lodger. On the application of Mr Hayes, the consideration of the claim was adjourned until the next morning. On Tuesday morning Mr William Tinsley, father of the claimant, appeared and stated that his son had the use of a sitting-room and bedroom, for which he paid lOs per week. During the past twelve months he had occupied the rooms possibly on ten Occasions. They were practically reserved for him and his furniture was in them. The family would use the sitting-room if they were pressed for accommodation, but the °ailment would have it entirely to himself whenever be liked. The bedroom might also be used by the family, in the event of sickness, or of some unexpected visit. The Barrister: I urn very sorry; I cannot allow this vote, because it seems to me this declaration with regard to the sitting-room is not correct. The only room be has is the bedreom, and even then you take it upon yourself to use it whenever you like. INSUFFICIENT VALUE. Mr. 'James Cecil Locker claimed a lodger vote in respect of a bedroom and sitting-room. He stated that Mr aud Mrs Locker, two sons and three daughters, occupied the house, which had five her rooms and two sitting-rooms. The Barrister: This is not value enough. Mr Sanders: fie has the exclusive right to the principal rooms in the house. The Barrister : No, I cannot allow it. "A TREAT FOR LANDLORDS." During the hearing of a case in which the rent book was in question, Mr Sanders said the landlord was on the "other side" in politics and he would have had a difficulty in getting him to attend the Court. The Barrister : You can always get those people by issuing a witness summons. In the case under n,itice the claimant said he repeatedly asked the landlord to place his name in the rent book but he kept putting it oil. The alteratioh was, however,made in time to qualify him for the vote.

The Barrister: When was that done. The Tenant: A month since. Mr Woodcock: The landlord's son certified that the alteration was made twelve months ago. The Barrister : No, I cannot allow that. I won't have an}thing of that sort. When the Court was resumed on Tuesday morning, the Barrister again referred to the case and said there had been an attempt to deceive the Court. Two dis- tinct statements were made by different persons. The tenant said the alteration was made a month ago, perfectly innocently,because he evidently did not know what the effect would be. The effect was that he didn't get his vote. The lanulord's son appeared evidently under the impression that he was going to support the claim for the vote by asserting that the alteration was made a long time ago. Tbe book had been marked 1912 and it was altered to 1911. He didn't believe that story, and did not know whether he ought not to deal with the witness. It Was a very serious matter if landlords and their representatives were going to attend and make what be was perfectly satided in that case was absolute misrepresentation, to put it mildly. He did not know whether he ought to take proceedings or not. Mr Sanders said he was not defending such conduct in any shape or form, hut he visited such house some months ago, and he obtained the information which was given by the landlord's son. He did not think there was deliberate misrepresentation. The Barrister : But you didn't see the alteration made. Mr Sanders: I was so clear that a mistake had been made that I at once made a note of it in my register for this claim to be brought forward. The Barrister: You mace a note in your register on January 2nd? Mr ganders : No, when I went round. Mr Sanders further expressed Lae opinion that the tenant made a slip of the tongue when he said the book was altered a month ago. 'the Barrister: I showed him the alteration and asked him when it was done, and he said "A month ego" Mr Sanders : I dou't believe in bringing false evidence. I won't be a party to it in any shape or form. I believe these to be respectable people who would not deliberately mislead the Court. The Barrister: First of all the landlord had no busi- ness to make the alteration. He ought to have supplied a new hook. I want this to be known, because I shall deal very severely with cases of this kind another time and disallow the votes. Whenever a landlord lets premises to a new tenant or changes the tenancy he must give a fresh hook to the DOW tenant and let the I thing be done in a perfectly straightforward manner. That is all I have to sty. Mr Hayes : lam much obliged to your Honour for those remarks. I have mentioned the matter before and there is not the slightest doubt it has been the practice in W'arrington. I have a case in my office where a man had only been a tenant for six months abil he got the landlord to give him a note that he had been in for eighteen months. Mr Sanders: I think Mr Hayes makes rash statements Mr Hayes : He does not make any rash statements I can show you the note. The Barrister : I have bad some cases of this kind and I have been wondering whether to take proceedings or not. Mr Sanders : Mr Hayes made a statement yesterday that rent books had been manufactured and " cooked for this reason, and I don't like it. The Barrister: I rather fancy I have had some evidence myself In this Court that I came to the con- clusion had been "cooked. Mr Sanders : I can vouch for the honourable inten- tions of the firm Mr Hayes referred to yesterday. I am not going to be a party to "cooking," in any shape or form. I would not waste your Honour's time. The Barrister : It is Dot a question of you or of the other agents. It is a question of whether the tenants, having ascertained what their position is, do try to do these things, with the landlord's assistance. div.p: Flag-Flying. Sir,—When will our worthy Corporation and its officials understand that flags are made to be flown in the day and not at night? When some local event requires the recogni- tion of hoisting, the flags are kept up night and day in all weathers until they become tattered and disreputable rags. The practice is slovenly, bad form, and uneconomical. The routine of Government offices is to hoist the flags at 8 a.m. and pull them down at sunset, and this plan should be adopted locally. In boisterous weather small size or storm flags should be used.— Yours, etc.. UNION JACK.

div.head: Harvest Thanksgivings (?)
div.p: Harvest Thanksgivings (?)

Sir,—l have been much interested in the discussion that has been carried on in various papers as to the reasonableness or otherwise of holding Harvest Festivals. If the clergy decide to hold the services might not the enclosed be added to the harvest hymn?

Tune—" e plough the fields and scatter:" We plough the waters daily To salve a little grain To decorate the churches, (They sometimes pray for rain!) We sing our harvest anthem Tho' stricken sore at heart, The parson must have wages. So we must act our part. Chorus—" All good gifts around us," &c.,— Yours faithfully, RAINPROOF. Paltry Progress.

Sir,—l feel that I must congratulate Mr. Dukes upon the great improvement of the tone and quality of his last letter. One can deal better with argument than assertion. But after reading his letter carefully and weighing up the situation as I see it, I can- not say that I feel at all convinced that strikes settle any differences under our present regime of capitalist production. In fact, I see a partial admittance by Mr. Dukes himself of this fact. At the outset he makes a disclaimer that "strikes are a means not a remedy." I believe lam right if I say that Marxian economists agree that labour is expropriated to the extent of at least two- thirds of what it produces. Now I ask myself, if labour organised can by the means of strikes gain for itself a part of what it produces but does not get from the capitalist class, why cannot it get the whole? .1 think that is a logical question. If labour by a strike, say this week, can get a 2s. rise and also, as Mr. Dukes asserts, the capitalist cannot raise prices, perhaps Mr. Dukes will tell how many strikes there need be, and how long it will bc before the worker will obtain that expro- priated surplus value of the Marxian cult. To me, in spite of its splendid tone and quality, Mr. Dukes' letter is a jumble. In the first place Mr. Dukes says that the capitalist cannot raise prices because of competition. He asserts that the capitalist urges that he cannot raise wages because of competition and yet in the same letter tries t 0 convince me that strikes will raise the price of labour. I ask Mr. Dukes if competition reduces the prices of the capitalist com- modities to the lowest possible level, does not the same law reduce the price of the worker to the lowest possible level? If Mr. Dukes' theorising is right I see nothing else for it. For myself I do not believe that competition operates to its fullest extent in either case. Certainly not in the capitalist case. The capitalist, owning the tools of production,and possessing greater knowledge of economics than the worker, has been in a better position to organise the production of commodities. If he cannot, the word monopoly has no meaning. The worker has no means of monopolising his labour power. All the forces obtainable have been used to reduce his wage to as low as possible. If the worker gains a rise i‘n wages improved machinery is intro- duced so as to reduce the amount of human labour necessary. The strike is only a cessation of production and in these days of concentrated production does anyone believe that the capitalists fear a strike? Even a strike in itself operates against the worker. If we cease to produce, we do not cease to consume. Cessation of production means scarcity of commodities. Scarcity of commodities means a rise in prices and in these days of monopoly we are lucky indeed if prices resume their normal,after production has been resumed. Considering this factor alone it is a question if the workers, assuming they get a rise in wages, come out of a con- flict with the balance on their side. Not con- sidering these things however, I believe it is an economic fallacy to say that strikes are necessary to maintain a wage necessary for a bare subsistence. The capitalist is no fool. He knows that workers living under the border line of subsistence are not a good invest- ment.A worker half fed is not a good worker. To me the strike is an insane weapon leaving only death and misery in its trail. I am firmly convinced that so long as the upper classes possess political and economic power the workers' position will remain as it is Mr. H. D. Lloyd, the great American anti-' trustist, says, IlThe public that submits to' the wars upon itself of coal strikes and coal trusts forfeits all rights to the name of American people. It is not a people, only a collection of persons, a national mob of persons living in economic anarchy. When we become civilised in- dustrially . . . we will tolerate either in coal or anything else no monopoly except our own monopoly, that of a people supply- ing at cost." It would be discourteous if I closed my letter without saying a word about Mr. Baguley's remarks. I may say that I am in entire agreement with what he suggests. If the workers want to use their power let them use their purchasing power. I have said before in the "Examiner " that the whole trouble lay in allowing a few of the community to supply us with our material needs. We need houses for shelter. \I re need food and clothing, but we allow any- one to control the supply of these things. I believe the future action of the workers should be in acquiring the control of the supply of their needs instead of ignorant revolt against a system of owner- ship which they continue to support. I may be uttering a heresy but I believe that the ownership of these things will gradually pass out of the hands of the present owners. The speed will depend on how fast the people understand their true economic position. I think it will be sound economics for those who believe they understand to try to acquire possession of at least some of the things necessary. For instance, it, say, 100 people thought that the present housing accommodation was unsatisfactory, they could find no difficulty in supplying them- selves with decent houses. Having got into their own houses, why not a communal bread and coal supply? This would be more sensible and scientific than strikes.—l am Yours &c., LABOR 01INIA VINCIT. •

div.head: CHESHIRE SOCIETY WEDDING.
div.p: CHESHIRE SOCIETY WEDDING.

SIR RICHARD BROOKE'S HEIR MARRIED A picturesque wedding of considerable local interest took place at St. George's Church, Hanover-square, London on Saturday, when Mr. Richard Christopher Brooke, Scots Guards, only son of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., and Lady Brooke, of Norton Priory, Runcorn, Cheshire, led to the altar Miss Marran Dorothy limes, cad}, daughter of the la.e Mr. Arthur Charles Innes, of Dromantine, Co. D•twn, and cousin of the Marquis and Marchioness cf Ailesbury. The service was fully choral, nod the fine church was beautifully decorated with white lilies and other white flowers intermixed with palms and foliage. The ceremony was performed by the Rector if the parish, the Rev. Norman Thicknesse, who was assisted by the bridegroom's cousin, the Rev. Gerald Halsey. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. Arthur C. hues, and very well she looked in her weoding robe of silver brocade, trimmed with old Brussels lace, and from the shoulders there fell a long train cf the same lace mounted on silver gauze. Her veil was of plain tulle and covered a crown cf real orange flowers in her hair, and she carried a bouquet of white carnations, lilies, aid white heather.

In attendance upon the bride was her cousin, Vie r•oung Earl of Cardigan (son of the Marquis and Marchioness of Ailesbury), who acted as page, and wore a picturesque Elizabethan co,tume of pale blue s.tin, with silk hose, and I,ce ruffles at wrists gni neck, while he also wore pale blue satin shoes orna- mented with paste buckles, and to him the bride gave a pearl scarf pin as a keepsake of the happy day There were also five bridesmaids, all children, the Ladies Ursula and Rosemary Brudenell-Bruce (daughters of the Marquis and Marchioness of Aiies- bury), cousins of the bride, Miss Crawley, Miss Julyar Cra ley, and Mis.s Patiet ce Crawley cousins of the bridegroom, wh were dressed alike in quaint high- waisted frocks of 'cream Liberty satio, with short puffed sleeves and long-ended sasbn of pa'e blue satin tied igh up under the arms. In tht-ir hair they wore pretty caps of pearl net, and they carried bouquets of shaded rises, and wore blue enamel and pearl pendants the gift of the bridegroom. At the conclusion of the ceremony the Marchioness of Aileshury held a reception at '29, Park-lane, lent by Mr. and Mrs. Bornby Lewis, and later in the day Mr. ard Mrs. It. C. Brooke bit for the Continent, where they e ill sperd their honeymoon. The bride's travelling costume was in fawn-evloured silk shan- tung, strapped with black satin. nod she also wore a larne picture hat tritium d at one side with a large yr llow wing.

A pretty wedding, in which considerable interest was taken, was solemnized at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Monday when Mr. W. Hewitt Dutton, son of Mr. and Mrs. Dutton, 302, Lovely-lane, was married to Miss Sara Silcock, daughter of Mrs. Silcock, of Forster- street. The bride is well known as a soprano vocalist and has achieved success in amateur opera as well as on the concert platform. She is a member of the Warrington Musical Society. The marriage service was conducted by the Rev. W. Reid. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac., was at the organ and played choice selections, the bridal party leaving the church to the strains of Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." The bride who was given away by her uncle, Mr. David Siicock, of Glazebury, was handsomely attired in a slate coloured silk voile dress, trimmed with ivory lace and chiffon. She also wore a black picture hat and carried a bouquet of lilies and white roses. She was attended by Miss Edie Tyson who Wore a pretty gown of cream serge and large black and white picture hat. Her bouquet was composed of lilies and pink roses. Mr. E. R. Roberts, of Runcorn, acted as best man. A reception was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall, a large number of guests attending. The wedding cake was made and presented by Mr. Joseph Hannan. Later Mr. and Mrs. Dutton left for North Wales where the honeymoon b• being spent. They were the recipients of many handsome presents.

div.head: WARRINGTON CANINE SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON CANINE SOCIETY.
Distribution of Cups and Prizes.

Members of the Warrington Canine Society met at the Lion Hotel, on Thursday evening for the distri- bution of the cups and special prizes gained at the eighth local show held in July. Mr Pennington, of Newton-le-Willows, handed the awards to the success- ful competitors as follows :—Colonel Edelsten's challenge cup for the hest dog, Mr V V Davies, Stockton Heath, with his retriever Bircbdale Banker ; Sir Gilbert Greenall's cup for the best bitch, Mrs Pennington, of Newton-le-Willows, with Woodhead Chocolate Mite ; Mr F W Wareing's cup for the best sporting dog, Mr J Heywood's, Sankey Joko ; Mr W A Leslie's cup for the beat Airedale, Mr J Lowe's Prim- rose Bob ; Messrs Carter's challenge cup for the best pup bred by an exhibitor, Mr Townley's Galliarcrs Double. Mr Pennington congratulated the society on the useful work it was doing and appealed to the members to give it stronger support. Short speeches were delivered by several members, including Mr Sanderson, Mr Astill, Mr Townley and Mr F White (Secretary). A few members' matches took place, Mr F Townley officiating as judge. Mr Eleywood's wire terrier Sankey Joko beat Mr F White's fox terrier Badger Knight. Ti.e Society will hold its next show on Boxing Day.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
The Season's Prospects.

The devotees of this winter sport are now arranging for a season which should prove one of the best on record. The failure of the British Olympic Council, and their advisers, to send a fully representative team to Stockholm will not be forgotten, ard all true sportsmen should now set about the task of preparing for the next Olympiad which is to be held at Berlin in 1016. Local enthusiasts were grievously disappointed that the claims of Chris Vose and lierbert Holbrook, to represent the United Kingdom, were overlooked by the people responsible for the Stockholm debacle, but it is up to them now to see that a repetition is avoided. Warrington Athletic Club have arranged to hold their annual general meeting at the pavilion near the foot- ball ground. on Thursday next at 730 p.m. and as they are contemplating an ambitious programme for the summer, as well es the winter, this meeting should be of the greatest interest to ail amateur athletes within 10 miles of the clubs' headquarters. Members and intending members should take the earliest opportunity of acquainting themselves with the details of the various running, jumping, cycling Scc competitions under consideration ; suitable suggestions will be welcomed. Those intending to follow cross country running should note that Easter falls early this season and an earlier start than usual is advisable to avoid the end of the season rush, Novices should find much to interest them in the many races which are being promoted for their class in the early part of the season. St Helens and District C.C.A. are holding their novice and intermediate class races for teams on January 11th next, i.e. two months earlier than last season, and are ft lo arranging three combined or league runs. The West Lancashire C C.A. hold their general meeting at the Bee Hotel, Liverpool, on Tues- day next at 7.30 p.m., the dates; suggested for their competitions are December 7th. Novice team race, January 25th or February Ist. Senior and Junior championship and according to existing rules the latter are the qualifying races for the Northern championship, February 15th. The National championship will be managed by the Midland C.C.A. A meeting of the clubs bas suggested March Ist for the race. The international will probably be held in France about March 15th. Novices should start eatly and remember that clean living and clear thinking will be factors towards success.

div.head: WATER POLO. WARRINGTON-v. ST. HELEKS.
div.p: WATER POLO. WARRINGTON-v. ST. HELEKS.

A fair number of spectators assembled in the Corpora- tion Baths, Legn-streat on Thursday evening to witness the splendid triumph of the locals over St Heler s in a match under the auspices of the Liverpool and District Water Polo and Squadron League, Third Division. The teams were :—Warrington: A Jolley. S Ince, and L Graham, H Furnival, S Roberts, J 'sanders and It Pepper. St Helens : J Rimmer, L Woods and R Clare, C Hull, P Rail, W Cha.nock and T Ball. The referee was Mr J Peers, Widnes. Prior to the game is f.. 0 yards handicap organised by the Whitecross social and recreation club wvs decided There were 15 entries and alter many exciting heats, the final winners were: 1, H 6isson. 2, W DJNning, 3, J 1 Furuival, 4. W Sisson. THE GAME. Warrington, although defending the deep end, had by far the best of the first few minutes. The visitors played hard and got dangerously near the home goal but they could not beat the clever local custoslian. The Warrington forwards subjected the Sr. Helens goal to a hot bombardment and if the visitors had not had such a sturdy eefence' there is no doubt that thc homesters would have bad at least five goals in the fist half. Rimmer kept his goal well and was loudly applauded forndany really fine Saves. Close On the interval Pepper receiv•-d on the right, and with incred- ible swiftresa sent the ball into the net. Half-time : Warrington, one goal ; St Helen; nil. On resuming, Warrington had matters practically all their own way, the forwatds showing splendid torus and keen judgment. Sanders received and with a quick orer-arm delivery passed to Pepper who aimed straight and beat the visitor's custodian all along. The local supporters were very enthusiastic with this lead of tao goals to nil but their enthudiasm knew no bounds when, from the centre the Warrington forwards forged up the bath and again Pepper scored with a rapid shot which crashed into the corner of the net, Rimmer being hopelessly beaten. About three minutes before time. P Hall received well down the bath and registered the first goal for St. Helens. Just before time Pepper again scored for Warrington amidst the prolonged applause of the spectators. Final :—Warrington 4 goals, St. Helens 1 goal.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 14, 1912.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 14, 1912.
PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There are many pleasing features in the programme submitted at the Hippodrome this week and as usual this popular house has been crowded nightly by patrons who can rely on the excellent judgment of the man- agement to provide all that is good in the variety world. Mr. Herbert Darnley's Company appear in the (..xcruciatingly funny sketch " Private Putts." There is an icceptahie smattering of tragedy in .the theme but the humorous s,tuations are the most salient parts of the production. Mr. Jack Witliaws, as the private, causes roars of laughter with his witty sallies and if the sketch is lacking in any part, success is assured by tis untiring efforts. We have witnessed some thriding pefurinance. by equiliblists but as yet we must hive the palm to Great Scott who has so successfully enreitained the audiences this week by his daring antics on the ladder—a neat, clever, and daring pertoimance. A wonderfui stage spectacle is. provided by Main in's Marvellous Foun- tains Th,re must ha hundreds of jets for the wa(er effects produced, but the excellence of the entertainment is considerably enhanced by toe varie-coloured electric lights which are focussed on the playing fountains and the nuwercui coicurs blend so beautifully together !hat the result rtruinds ore cf Arcadia. Cl e and Raggs give us a very accept- able comedy and juggling tuin and in audition to scoring with thcir tricky feats, the humorous in- cidents provided I y me cf tk e enterta nieg couple, are mot laughable in their utter absurdity. Billy Sinips( n is billed as an Australian character comedian but we failed to see the cowei(y iu the very senti- mental song about a cigar. There was another lively discussion at the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians on Wednesday on the question of the use of stimulants in the Union Hospital. Mr E L Bent presided and there were also present :—Mrs Simpson, Revs T R Matthews and A M Mitchell, Dr Murray, Messrs A J Jolley (deputy-chair- man), J Billinge, Cr Mather, A Brooks, W C Brooks, ft Lee, W Flanagan, J A Rushworth, ft I Pertridge (assistant clerk), 0 Moss (assistant master), and C E Lawrsnce (superintendent of Cottage Homes). The Clerk awed hit it ens gnnectssery, so far as his judgment vent, to arise et register at all in the Infirmary, because the ,equisition tee k of st res and supplies was addl. le t °cord. Ile (the speaker) looked at that rsqii.aii ion book at the last rneetit g of the Souse Com- teis ana found that, although spirits and beer were mentioned, no quantities were specified. Looking thrie,gh tle book, he noticed that no quantities seetnef to have I een specified for something like a year pest. Certainly the quantities of champagne, which seemed to have teen -newly introauced lot, tile fr.flimac_i, had bean specified. He was gerfectly satedisd that the master aid all be ought to do in keeping unorga of the stimulants as part of the stores. He was als sure that the medical men were perfectly honourable in the matter, but at the same time it was a matter more or less of business. It was public) expenditure, and as the expenditure was very large, it was theright of every menther of the Board and of every ratepayer to have some hire of the qualities used. The Rev. A. M. MITCH ICLL Jlor, hear, as well as

The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Mitchell was labouring under a great mistake. If he would only tat,e the trouble to consult the books, be would find that a record was kept of all the stimulants that were recom- mended for the patients,' as ordered by the medical officer. Mr Mitchell said there was only the master's book containing the general quantities and that there was no book containing the quantities issued for each patient. He (the Chairman) said the quantities for each patient were kept in a book and that the spirits and ail stimulants were under the control of the master and were not kept in the doctor's quarters. The bottles were taken to the stores, each marked with the quantity required, the name of the patient and number of the bed, and when they had been tilled they were placed in a basket which was not unlocked until it was delivered to ths nurse who had charge of the ward. "I think" concluded the Chairman " that you only bring this forward for the sake of advertising yourself." The Rev A M MITCHELL: Mr Chairman- The CHAIRMAN : Excuse me, it is nothing else. It is westing the time of the Board to bring such thing as this forward. If you would only go to the offices and make inquiries, you could get ail the information you required. But you wont. You want to come here and raise the question before the Board, so that it will get into the public Press. I don't withdraw it. I say it is advertising-- Ihe Rev A M MITCHELL : Is this maintaining the dignity of the chair ? Mr RUSHWOR.TH : It is a waste of time.
The CIIAIRNIAN : I leave it to the. mac-Of the mem- bers to say what they like, but I think it is disgraceful that these things should be brought before the Board and time wasted.

The Rev A M MlTcitxt.L : You have the resolution. Will you kindly put it? Mr JOLLEY said the matter was not quite so trivial as the members supposed. There was a question of principle behind it. Mr. Mitchell had stated his point of view with great moderation that morning, but he either misunderstood or had not taken the trouble to investigate the conditions. The matter was considered by the House Committee in a somewhat informal way last Friday afternoon, and it led to the question of the Workhouse accounts being discussed at some length. He was bound to agree with the Chairman in the main that on that particular point the statements made by Mr Mitchell, if they were not definitely contraverted, were liable to mislead people outside. It was almost suggested that there was something wrong in their methods of book-keeping. On former occasions Mr Mitchell, like some other people, had criticised with considerable severity—perhaps with more severity than knowledge—the number of cfficials maintained in that ' and other Unions. It was a kind of cry that was raised and occasionally appealed to a certain class of ' people outside, just about election time, to denounce officialism and to point with the finger of derision at the excessive expenditure of public money I on officials' salaries. It was very cheap to do that. They were bound to have officials if they were to have efficient work done, and it was very easy to raise a point of that kind. About five years .ago, the whole question of Workhouse accounts was considered by a Departmental Committee. Mr. Mitchell was not the only person who had any real interest in seccring efficiency and economy of administration. Many Guardians and officials were equally desirious of securing it. As a result of the deliberations of the Departmental Committee, a number of modifications were introduced, tending to diminish, so hr as it could be done with safety, the number of books to be kept. Mr. Mitchell bad suggested that they should go in for more hook-keeping. There was no suggestion that any useful purpose would be served by the keeping of the register. It would merely enable Mr. Mitchell ,to quote figures in support of the kind of statements they had heard that morning—figures which be might easily obtain, if he chose to devote a few 'minutes to the task of examining the records that were in the master's office. He (Mr. Jolley) hoped that the Board would not pass the resolution which was merely a suggestion to increase ihe clerical work of the doctor and the master whose time ought to be devoted to very much better purposes. The system of book-keep- ing and checking of stores was the best that could be devised by a committee of competent expens. If it was to be criticised,it ought to he critised by competent persons and not in the somewhat amateurish manner which bad been suggested that morning. The Rev AM MrrcHELL,referring to the comments of the Chairman, said he was so familiar with that sort of treatment that he treated it with the contempt it deserved.
--- --. The CHAIRMAN: 1 think it is given oftener then received. -- - -

The Rev A M MITCHELL: You said a book is kept— that there is a record. If my memory does not deceive me, the Clerk distinctly told us at the last meeting that there was no such record—that the only record was the requisition book kept by the master. The ASSISTANT CLERK explained that what the Clerk stated was that the total quantity distributed weekly was shown in the master's provision book, but not the quantity allowed to each patient.

The ( HAIRMAN : I explained that there was another book with the quantities allowed to each patient. The Rev A M MITCHELL: At one Board meeting we are told one thing and at another meeting another. Mr A BROOKS said that what the Clerk said was that there was no book specially kept for giving the record of stimulants. Perhaps he was a little remiss in not saying there was a book which gave the doctor's medical extras and that book would give all that Mr Mitchell asked for—chops, steaks, fish and everything. The Rev A M MITCHELL said he was only asking that the standing orders which provided that the various books should be laid upon the table, should be obeyed. It was a very modest request. The CHAIRMAN : But you asking that a special book shall be kept and the quantities of spirits and beer con- sumed in the institution recorded.

The Rev A M MITCHELL : If you say there is such a record, I say " Let us have that book put on the table." This resolution has been introduced on the assumption that there is no book kept. On a vote being taken the resolution was defeated by S votes to 2, the supporters of the resolution being Mrs Simpson and the Rev A M Mitchell.

The lies, A M MITCHELL then proposed a further resolution :—" That a return be prepared shewing the quantities and cost under each head, of spirits, wines and beer charged to the Union between July Ist 1911 and June 30th 1912." He said it was nearly two years since they had such a statement submitted to them, The previons statement was very helpful and it was prepared with very consider- able care. It showed that the amount expended on stimulants in the Infirmary was about £l2O a year. Mr W C BROOKS : No, no. I rise to correct Mr Mitchell. It was not the amount spent in the Infirmary but the amount spent in the whole Union. The CHAIRMAN : I think Mr Brooks is correct.

Mr MATHER : These wrong impressions get into the papers and the public talk. The Rev A M MITCEIELL: .£l2O is a very large sum, which ever way you look at it. We were told by the doctor that more would be expended aud that we might expect heavier payments. I made inquiries at the time from other Unions and ascertained that the Ormskirk Union—which is a very large Union—expended some- thing under £3 a year on stimulants. There is a wonderful disparity, whether Mr Brooks is correct or not, between .£3 and £l2O. It may be that the amount now is considerably larger. We have also a new doctor and we don't know what his methods are, as regards the administration of stimulants. Mr A BROOKS seconded.

The CHAIRMAN said the resolution was perfectly in order but it would be much easier for the clerks and everyone eke concerned if Mr Mitchell would ask for the return at the end of the half year. After some discussion with the Chairman, Mr MuctieLL agreed to extend the period fur which the return was asked to September 30th next. Mr MATHER: I rise to a point of order. This is a conversation between the Chairman and the man who is submitting the resolution. I feel sure that if you, Mr Chairman, would leave it to the members to discuss this before you commence to discuss it with the mover of the resolution, we should get on and nut lose as much time. (Hoer, bear.) The CHAIRMAN: As Chairman of the Board I have the liberty of speaking before or after the discussion. Mr JOLLEY said he should vote against the res &Akin whatever happened, because if the return were prepared it would simply be the text for another temperance dies° tation of a more or less relevant character aud he thought they might well he spared any more discussions on that theme. Some of them had been "fed up " with it for some time. Secondly he opposed the resolution for a much more important reason which no doubt would arouse the decisive ridicule of the Rev. A. M. Mitchell— because it affected the interests of the sic c po .r. He str•mgly objected not merely to their own time AA a , Boara being wasted as it had been repeatedly of late, but for the more imtoriant reason that the tendency of that kind of thing was to *pet pressure on the medical officer to adopt a treatu,etit of the sick poor that was not in uccordance with their best judgment in order' to avoid the vulgar criticisms to which they were occasioually exposed. (flew., hear). That, in the , interests ot the sick poor, was a thing they OuOtt stroagly to deprecate end set their faces e lle , hoped Mr. A. Brooks would not assume he was associa- ting him with that policy. Mr. A. BROOKS : You can du whet you like. Mr JOLLEY' : Mr Brooks end I hays known each other for many pare. We know that Mr Brooks lies , for many years taken a loyal and real interest in the good administration of the institution, but I am sorry to say that cannot he said of Mr Mitchell. the Rev s. H MITCHELL : 'Hest is is libel. Mr JOLLEY : Mr Mitchell got up this morning and sail the expenditure in this direction was very large. That is a gr, as mis-statement. The expenditure, on the figures placed before us this morning, works out at 2d per week per head of the sick poor in this hospital. Dues any sane member of this Board grudge expendi- ture of 2,1 per week ler head for the restoration to health of the sick poor ? If Mr Mitchell wants an advertisemeut, let him have it in this way--that he grudges the expenditure of 21 a week for the benefit of the sick poor. The Rev A M MITCHELL : That is very funny. Mr A BROOKS said Mr Jolley was quits right in stat- ing that there was an idea to put a little pressure on the medics' officer. He thought medical officers often ran to the easiest way in that matter—to the way in which patients liked to be treated—that was a little of something " short "to help them to get better. There were, however, hospitals where alcoholic stimulants were not used and the results were better than, or as good as in hospitals where they were used. It was not for that reason that he seconded the resolution, but it was as well to say something on the other side. He did not think Mr. Mitchell and certainly' he (the speaker) did not grudge the 2d. a week—in fact it did not work out at 2d a week, because the £l2O a year included a laree amount for stimulants given outside the hospital. He wag sure no member of the Board was mean enough to I grudge anything of that amount to the sick poor. What he and others thought was that other treatment might not have the same amount of danger in its after-conse- quences that the administration of alcohol had. On the resolution being put to the meeting, five voted for it and flee against, the Chairman giving his casting vote against the resolution. Mr. MATHER : I am against all these fads. lam sick of it.

The CHAIRMAN: Such resolutions tend to make people think there is something going on thst ought not to be, in the institution. I don't know whet'ier you fancy the officials are getting the stimulants. DECREASE IN OUT-RELIEF. The Rev A M MuctigLL called attention to a return issued by Mr Lowry (Local Government Board Inspector) showing that the number in receipt of out- door relief in the Union on January Ist. 1912, was 900 as against 1203. the average number relieved on January Ist, 19J7 to 1911. It was therefore somewhat surprising to find that the amount put down for out-relief in the Clerk's eatimkte was £2,800 as compared with £2,720 for the preceding half-year. In view of Mr Lowry 's public statement and of the statistics showiug that the number who were receiving out-door relief was decreasing, they might have some explanation as to why more money was being asked for. The ASSISTANT CLERK :More adequate relief is being given to these 0/IFO3B. That is the simple explanation. Mr MATHER : I take it the money is teing asked for, but it is not going to be epsnt unless it is really requisite. The relief committees in every district have been a great deal more liberal in the rate of out-relief than formerly, but anything that is going to help the poor, tee sick and the needy, gets Mr Mitchell's severe criticism from beginning to end. The Rey A M MITCHELL: No, no. Don't speak like that please.
, Mr MATHRR : He has been criticising the Clerk's estimating for this money. The relief committees ask for it—

-The Rev A 111 MITCHELL : This is not in order. It is personal. Mr MATHER : The relief committees have this money at their disposal. The Clerk is bound to make provision for ninitever the relief committees give to outside casts. It is a well known fact that within twelva months the outdoor relief given to poor people has been inoreased,greatly to the benefit of the sick and poor.
The Rev A M MITCHELL: Not in Mr Lowry's dis- trict. It has decreased. _

Mr W C BROOKS : I submit the whole thing is out of order. The estimate has been before this Board sod adopted. Wh) should we re-open the discussion on it ? Mr. A BROOKS pointed out that mainly owing to the coal strike, the expenditure ca relief dining the last half year had been abnormal and the Clerk was not going to he caugnt "napping "again. Mr MATHER : lie knows his business and he attends to it.

The CHAIRMAN said Mr Mitchell would be quite aware that the committee in his own district had been more literal in the distribution of outdoor relief of late, and he believed that applied all round. Mr JOLLEY said be failed to find any statement in l‘fr Lowry's return that outdoor relief bad decreased. Mr Mitchell had overlooked the fact that the return referred to the number of recipients on a particular day, and that.! as a.very fluctuating quantjty.

NOTES BY " OYALIST." Saturday's football gave the local optimists a Lit of a jolt. Warrington only lost nari owlv at Leigh, but they performed inglorious y, and the A" team had the unpleasant experience of a licking at home before a crowd which expected something vastly different. If it is any consolation to us there is the fact, that the optimists of Wigan and Oldham mast be feelirg a lot worse. Personally, I found the shock to Warrington's prestige quite sufficient. We were led to. believe that the team was much better than the Huddersfield result indicated, and might reasonably be expected to show Leigh a thing or two. Well, I went to Leigh and returned disillusioned. Two very poor teams were on view and tire Wirepullers were the poorer of the two. Had they shown a spark of cleverness in the back divisi ,n they must have won, but I verily believe that if they had played till now they would not have scored a try. The attempts at combination would have made a Itylands' man blush! The match was a scrappy scramble from beginning to end. Leigh won because they knew enough to work their way to the line, and stay there till they scored. The tactics of the winners were those of a generation ago, but they sufficed to beat Warrington. -- No doubt it is early in the season to expect very much in the way of combination, but it was not want of practice that made Warrington so feeble on the attack. It was rotten half-back play first, foremost, and all the time. The threequarters were not brilliant by a lot, and they made a few mistakes, but they could look down on the half backs. Leigh had a couple of unknown juniors behind the scrum. Even they were superior to the Warrington pair, who undid all the 'good work of a very active lot of forwards.

It bears the inscription: DONUM JOHANN'S BOOTH COLONELLI ET RECTORIS HUJUS EMPORII DE WARRINGTON 1647, which would read in English, "The gift of John Booth, governor of this market town of Warrington, 1647." A new fire bell was provided when the Court House was demolished in 1855 and as it was placed upon the west end of the Market Hall hung upon the site which its predecessors had occupied for centuries. Two " relics of the old Court House are preserved in the entrance hall of the Museum. One of the quatre-foil stones, formerly part of a Friary pillar and after- wards part of a pillar that supported the Court House tower, now serves as a base for the central gas bracket. To the left of the doorway is a carved stone which bears a pair of shears such as are used in sheep shearing with the letters T.B. This had a place in the wall of the old Court House. A photograph taken during demolition is also preserved which shows the quatre-foil pillars. A.M. (To be Continued). • CHILDREN'S CORNER, Conducted by UNCLE CALEB.

The practice of altering rent books called forth further strong comments from the Barrister. During the hearing of a claim brought forward by Mr Sanders on Monday morning, the son of the landlord attended and stated on oath that the alteration of the name in the rent hook was made in January, 1911. He made the correction and inserted the date to emphasise it. The Barrister: You don't want any date to emphasise the correction of the Chritian name. Mr Sanders said the case was clearly one in which the son wanted the vote and got his mother, who was formerly the tenant, to transfer the souse in his name. The Barrister said he should watt to know why the landlord altered the book instead of giving tbe tenant a new one. Mr Sanders : Of course, he was not aware of the law. The Barrister : I am not satisfied with this, but you can bring more evidence if you like. At the evening sitting the tenant, Samuel Waring, of Windsor-street, gave evidence. He stated that a mistake was made in the rent hook and it was rectified.
